1  SCOPE
This NBCS (Part C/Section 5) deals with the structural use of plain, reinforced, and prestressed concrete.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
2 TERMINOLOGY
For the purpose of this Section, the definitions given in accepted standards [C-5(1)] shall apply.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
3 MATERIALS
All materials used in plain, reinforced and prestressed concrete construction shall conform to Part B ‘Building Materials’ of this NBCS as available.

chunks.section_title: STRUCTRAL DESIGN USING PLAIN, REINFORCED AND PRESTRESSED CONCRETE
chunks.text:
4 STRUCTRAL DESIGN USING PLAIN, REINFORCED AND PRESTRESSED CONCRETE
The provision relating to design and general structural use of plain, reinforced and prestressed concrete, including on:
a) materials, including special concrete, workmanship, inspection and testing;
b) general design consideration;
c) special design requirements for structural members and systems; and d) structural design: limit state method.
shall be in accordance with good practices contained in section 2, section 3, section 4 and section 5 of the good practice [C-5(2)] and section 2, section 3 and section 4 of the good practice [C-5(3)].
NOTE — At the time of publication of this section, IS 456 and IS 1343 were under revision, with IS 1343 being amalgamated into IS 456. Once the revised IS 456 is published, it shall replace the provisions given in 4.
The informative Annex A to this Section suggests the updated list of materials and few tests.  Users are encouraged to investigate the possibility of applying the provisions given in Annex A which are listed in consonance with the provisions regarding materials in the good practice [C-5(2)].
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: STRUCTURAL SAFETY OF TALL REINFORCED CONCRETE (RC) BUILDINGS
chunks.text:
5 STRUCTURAL SAFETY OF TALL REINFORCED CONCRETE (RC) BUILDINGS
For criteria for structural safety of tall reinforced concrete (RC) buildings of heights greater than 50 m and less than 250 m, normally intended for use as residential, office and other commercial buildings, reference may be made to Annex E and accepted standard [C-5(4)].

A-3.2.3 Treated Water Appropriately treated water, conforming to A-3.3, from industrial, municipal and other sources can be used in concrete. A-3.2.4 Water Recovered from Processes in the Concrete Industry This includes:
a) water that was part of surplus concrete;
b) water used to clean the inside of the stationery mixers, mixing drums of truck mixer or agitators and concrete pumps; and c) process water from sawing, grinding and water blasting of hardened concrete. This water may be taken from:
1) Basins provided with suitable equipment that distributes the solid matter evenly throughout the water;
and 2) Sedimentation basins or similar installations, provided the water is left in the basin for a sufficient amount of time to allow the solids to settle properly. Water recovered from process in the concrete industry contains varying concentrations of very fine particles, the size of which is generally less than 0.25 mm. Water recovered from processes in the concrete industry or combined water can be used provided the following requirements are met:
i) The additional mass of solid material in the concrete resulting from the use of water recovered from processes in the concrete industry shall be less than 1 percent mass fraction of the total mass of aggregates present in the concrete; and ii) The amount of recovered water shall be spread as evenly as possible over a day's production. B-3.1.1 Procedure Slump flow test shall be carried out in accordance with the accepted standard [C-5(36)]. B-3.1.2 Classes of Slump-Flow and their Application There are three classes of slump-flow, as follows:
a) SF1 (slump flow 550 mm to 650 mm)  –  This class of SCC is appropriate for:
1) unreinforced or slightly reinforced concrete structures that are cast from the top with free displacement from the delivery point (such as slabs); and
2) casting by a pump injection system (such as tunnel linings), and 3) sections those are small enough to prevent long horizontal flow (example, piles and some deep foundations). b) SF2 (slump flow 650 mm to 750 mm) is suitable for many normal applications (example, walls, columns); and c) SF3 (slump flow 750 mm to 850 mm) is typically produced with a small maximum size of aggregates (less than 20 mm) and is used for vertical applications in structures having congested reinforcement, structures with complex shapes, etc. SF3 will often give better surface finish than SF2 for normal vertical applications but segregation resistance is more difficult to control. B-3.2   Passing Ability (Free from Blocking at Reinforcement) Passing ability describes the capacity of the fresh mix to flow through confined spaces and narrow openings such as areas of congested reinforcement without segregation. If there is little or no reinforcement, there may be no need to specify passing ability as a requirement. L-box test is generally carried out to check the passing ability and the procedure shall be in accordance with the accepted standard [C-5 (36)]. In this test, the height of the concrete left in the vertical section (h1) and at the end of the horizontal section (h2) is measured. The ratio of h2/h1 is calculated as the blocking ratio; which shall be between 0.8 and 1.0.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
B-3.3   Segregation Resistance (Stability) Segregation Resistance is the ability of fresh concrete to remain homogeneous in composition while in its fresh state. Segregation resistance is generally carried out using sieve test to check this property of fresh concrete. B-3.3.1  Procedure Segregation resistance (sieve) test shall be carried out in accordance with accepted standard [C-5(36)]. B-3.3.2  Test Results There are two classes of segregation resistance, namely SR1 and SR2. For SR1 class, segregation resistance should be above 15 percent and < 20 percent, and for SR2 it should be < 15 percent. SR1 is generally applicable for thin slabs and for vertical applications with a flow distance of less than 5 m and a confinement gap greater than 80 mm. SR2 is preferred in vertical applications if the flow distance is more than
5 m with a confinement gap greater than 80 mm in order to take care of segregation during flow. Segregation
resistance becomes an important parameter with higher slump-flow classes and/or the lower viscosity class, or if placing conditions promote segregation. If none of these apply, it is usually not necessary to specify a segregation resistance class. B-3.4 Viscosity Viscosity can be assessed by the V-funnel flow time. Concrete with a low viscosity will have a very quick initial flow and then stop. Concrete with a high viscosity may continue to creep forward over an extended time. NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
B-3.4.1 Procedure Viscosity by V-funnel test is carried out in accordance with accepted standard [C-5 (36)]. A V-shaped funnel is filled with fresh concrete and the time taken for the concrete to flow out of the funnel is measured and recorded as the V-funnel flow time. B-3.4.2 Test Results The viscosity is divided into two classes, namely V1 and V2. For V1 class, the time taken to pass the concrete from V-funnel shall be < 8 s and for V2 class, it shall be above 8 s and < 25 s.

Storage of constituent materials for SCC shall be same as that for materials for conventional concrete. However, as the SCC mix is more sensitive to variations, special precautions shall be taken for storage of aggregates, which should be properly stored to avoid cross-contamination between different types and sizes and protected from weather to minimize the fluctuation of surface moisture content and movement of fines. Ground stock should be PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 5 STRUCTURAL CONCRETE
stored in purpose-built partitioned bays, which should allow free drainage of excess moisture in the aggregates and rainwater. B-5.3 Mixing Equipment and Trial Mixes SCC shall be produced with efficient forced action concrete mixers. The time necessary to achieve complete mixing of SCC may be longer than for conventional concrete due to reduced frictional forces and to fully activate the superplasticizer. B-5.4 Formwork Formwork should be watertight and grout tight when placing SCC. The need to design the formwork for water tightness is greater than conventional formwork so as to avoid honeycombs and surface defects. The high fluid nature of SCC may lead to higher formwork pressure than conventional concrete, especially when the casting rate is high. As a result of the highly fluid nature of SCC, a high placement rate is likely and should be anticipated. Formwork designs, that accommodate the expected liquid head formwork pressure, can allow unrestricted placement rates and permit fast casting rate of the SCC. It is recommended to design the formwork for full liquid head. B-5.5 Curing Curing is essential for all concrete, and early protection of exposed surfaces is essential to preventing rapid moisture loss that could lead to plastic shrinkage cracking. The top-surface of elements made with SCC can dry quickly because of the increased quantity of paste, the low water/fines ratio and the lack of bleed water at the surface.

chunks.text:

Initial curing should therefore commence as soon as practicable after placing and finishing in order to minimize the risk of surface crusting and shrinkage cracks caused by early age moisture evaporation. B-6 ENGINEERING PROPERTIES B-6.1 General SCC and conventional concrete of similar compressive strength have comparable properties. B-6.2 Compressive Strength SCC with a similar water-cement ratio usually have a slightly higher strength compared to conventional concrete due to the lack of vibration giving an improved interface between the aggregate and hardened paste. B-6.3 Tensile Strength SCC may be supplied with any specified concrete grade. For a given concrete grade, the tensile strength may be safely assumed to be the same as the one for a conventional concrete as the volume of paste (cement + fines + water) has no significant effect on tensile strength. B-6.4 Static Modulus of Elasticity Increasing the paste volume may decrease the modulus of elasticity, Ec. As SCC has higher paste content than conventional concrete, some difference can be expected and the Ec may be somewhat lower and should be adequately covered by the safe assumptions in design. If SCC does have a slightly lower Ec than conventional concrete, in prestressing work, this will affect the relationship between the compressive strength and the camber due to pre-tensioning or post-tensioning. For this reason, careful control should be exercised over the strength at the time when the pre-tensioning and posttensioning strands or wires are released. B-6.5 Creep Due to the higher volume of cement paste, the creep coefficient for SCC may be expected to be higher than for conventional concrete of equal strength, but such differences are small and shall be covered by the safe assumptions in design.

B-6.6 Shrinkage As concrete compressive strength is related to the water-cement ratio, in SCC with a low water-cement ratio drying shrinkage reduces, but with increased cementitious content and increased water content the drying shrinkage and autogenous shrinkage can increase. B-6.7 Durability SCC is free from shortcomings due to improper compaction and result in consistently low and uniform permeability, offering less weak points for deleterious actions of the environment.

ANNEX C
(Foreword) HIGH PERFORMANCE CONCRETE C-1 GENERAL High performance concrete is a concrete whose ingredients, proportions and production methods are specifically chosen to meet special performance and uniformity requirements. The higher performance requirements may be:
Sl No. Higher Performance  Requirements Remarks/Applications (1) (2) (3) i) High resistance to deterioration of reinforced concrete due to carbonation This is to help achieve longer service life. This is particularly applicable in semi-arid regions ii) High resistance to chloride attack/ingress This is for longer service life of reinforced concrete exposed to severe chloride environment/coastal environment iii) High resistance to abrasion This may be required in concrete structures, like parts of hydraulic structures exposed to continuous abrasive action due to silt, such as spillways/glacis; and concrete pavements exposed to heavy traffic iv) High resistance to impact This may be required in structures like blast resistant structures and spillways v) Improvement in flexure and shear performance This is required in bridge girders, joints of RCC framed structure, shear walls, etc vi) High resistance to cracking due to shrinkage (plastic and drying shrinkage) This may be required in concrete/mortar used for repair of distressed concrete structures, etc High strength concrete generally improves performance of all above parameters. The concrete mix proportioning for high strength concrete may be carried out in accordance with the good practice [C-5(37)]. However, special measures are needed to further improve the specific performance requirements. As a guide, the measures given in C-2 may be adopted. For further details, expert literature may be referred.

chunks.text:
C-2 MEASURES FOR IMPROVING SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS C-2.1 Resistance to Carbonation Resistance to carbonation of concrete is dependent mainly upon:
a) Type of binder, content of binder and pH value of concrete; and PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 5 STRUCTURAL CONCRETE
b) Permeability of concrete. Addition of silica fume, GGBS and fly ash improve denseness and reduce permeability, thus increasing resistance to ingress of carbon dioxide and moisture (needed for carbonation). The addition of fly ash above 35 percent tends to lower the alkalinity, and thus the resistance to carbonation. Lower water-cement ratios and higher grades of concrete can be adopted to improve performance in this case. Minimum OPC content is essential for adequate carbonation resistance for different exposure conditions. Carbonation resistance can be checked by using accelerated carbonation tests (using 3 percent to 4 percent CO2 concentrations for minimum 70 days exposure) at mix proportioning stage. For quality assurance purpose, rapid tests like rapid chloride ion penetration test (RCPT), air permeability test or electrical resistivity test may be used. Their values may be established by correlation with accelerated carbonation test values at mix proportioning stage. C-2.2 Resistance to Chloride Ingress To improve performance of concrete exposed to chloride environment, two aspects need to be considered:
a) Total initial chloride content in concrete should be minimized; and b) Permeability of concrete should be low. Whereas chloride content of concrete can be controlled by checking chloride content of mix ingredients, the permeability of concrete can be reduced by careful selection of mix proportions and by use of supplementary cementing materials, either through use of blended cements like PPC and PSC or by direct addition of mineral admixtures, like fly ash, GGBS and silica fume.

ANNEX D
(Foreword and Clause C-2.4.1) DESIGN OF STEEL FIBRE REINFORCED CONCRETE D-1 GENERAL This Annex shall apply where steel fibres are used to improve the performance and capacity of reinforced and prestressed concrete structures. The design of steel fibre reinforced concrete (SFRC) at both the ultimate and serviceability limit states shall be based on the stress (σ) ≠ strain (ε) relationships for SFRC as specified in D-3.3 (see Note 1). Steel fibres shall not be relied upon in plastic hinge regions for strength requirements (see Note 2). Steel fibres shall not be relied upon at constructions joints for either serviceability or strength requirements. Design procedure in this clause is for steel-fibre-reinforced concrete with a softening classification only (see Fig. 1). Hardening SFRC and the use of synthetic fibres is beyond the scope of this annex. NOTES When using brittle fibres that rely on a fibre pull-out failure mechanism to obtain member ductility, care is required for cases where a significant number of fibres fracture or where fibres result in local crushing of the concrete due to the local forces imposed on the matrix by the fibres. Fibre fracture may occur where the bond between the fibre and the matric is high, and this is more likely in a high strength concrete combined with fibres of high bond capacity and of lower strength steels. The anchorage capacity of steel fibres may be lost in areas where crack widths exceed about 3.5 mm. Cracking of this magnitude can be expected in regions where plastic rotations are expected. D-2 DEFINITIONS For the purposes of this Annex the following definitions shall apply:
D-2.1 Crack Mouth Opening Displacement (CMOD) — The width of a crack shall be measured at its mouth in a flexural tensile test.

D-2.3  Steel Fibre Reinforced Concrete (SFRC) — A mixture of concrete and steel fibres. D-2.4  Hardening Behaviour — A material that displays an enhanced strength with increasing crack widths beyond that measured at the point of initial cracking of the cementitious matrix. D-2.5  Softening Behaviour — A material that exhibits a loss of strength upon cracking. D-2.6  Target Dosage — The specified quantity of fibres in kilograms per cubic metre of concrete (kg/m3). NOTE  — There is considerable discussion in the literature on whether the ends of the specimens should be fixed at each end, pinned at each end or fixed at one end and pinned at the other. The adoption of one pinned and one fixed end is a pragmatic decision between the ideal condition (fixed at each end) and limitations in manufacturing of specimens that are perfectly square at their ends for alignment within the testing machine. With both ends fixed any misalignment induces a moment in the specimen during gripping. This moment can induce a tensile stress on one side of the specimen, weakening the specimen. chunks.text: E-1.7  For buildings that do not conform to the prescriptive requirements of this Annex, a more rigorous procedure is necessary for design and review. E-2 - E-3 TERMINOLOGY For the purpose of this Annex, the following definitions shall apply. E-3.1 Building Height — The difference in levels between the base level of a building, at which inertia forces generated in the structure are transferred to the foundation, which then transfers these forces to the ground, and the highest level of a building, which is the roof of the topmost level which is structurally integral and continuous with the floor below (see also E-4). E-3.2 Connecting Structure — A structure that links two or more towers, except at the podium levels. NOTE — There are two distinctive types of connecting structures with each one requiring a different structural treatment, namely, (a) the connecting structure having the role of transferring gravity loads only and with no participation in the role of resisting the lateral loads on either of the towers; and (b) the connecting structure participating in the lateral load resisting structural system, where the two towers act together when one or both towers is subjected to lateral loads due to the interaction provided by the connecting tower. E-3.3 Core — An assembly of structural walls coupled with link elements and offering lateral stiffness in two orthogonal directions. E-3.4 Coupled Structural Wall Building — A building comprising of structural walls linked by in-plane beam elements, wherein the vertical and lateral loads are resisted by these structural walls, through axial load, in-plane bending moment and shear force, and the coupling action created by push-pull in the wall elements by framing action provided by link beams. E-3.5 Frame Building — A building comprising beams and columns, wherein the vertical and lateral loads are resisted by these elements through moment-frame action.

E-3.6 Gravity Columns — Vertical members that are intended to carry primarily the vertical loads arising out of the dead and imposed loads on the building, and do not participate in the lateral load resisting system. Such columns shall be capable primarily of carrying the gravity loads and additional induced loads while complying with the relative lateral deformation effects imposed on them during lateral earthquake shaking. E-3.7 Key Elements — The element such that its failure would cause the collapse of more than a limited area close to it. The limited area may be taken equal to 70 m2 or 15 percent of the area of the storey, whichever is lesser. If key elements exist, it is preferable to modify the layout so that the key element is avoided. E-3.8 Linking Beams (Also called coupling beams) —  Horizontal members spanning two (vertical) structural walls. E-3.9 Mixed Building or Hybrid Building — A building in which select primary elements resisting vertical and/or lateral loads comprise more than one material; composite elements comprising structural steel and reinforced concrete are common examples. E-3.10 Multi-Tower Structures Linked by Podium — Two or more towers above a common podium structure that are not separated by a movement joint at the podium level. E-3.11 Natural Period — The time taken (in seconds) by the structure to complete one cycle of oscillation in its natural mode of oscillation. E-3.12 Structural Systems and Sub-Systems E-3.12.1 Structural Wall System — A structural system comprising of inter-connected structural walls, wherein the vertical and lateral loads are resisted by the walls through axial load, in-plane bending moment and shear force. The wall elements are configured by a combination of structural wall elements connected integrally to a floor diaphragm.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: The wall elements form the primary lateral load resisting structural system for the building, and resist the loads imposed on them through axial, shear and flexural actions, and through coupling actions offered by the connecting link elements if provided. E-3.12.2 Moment Frame System — A structural system comprising (beam-column) frames and resisting the vertical and lateral loads. E-3.12.3 Moment Frame-Structural Wall System — A structural system comprising (beam-column) frames and structural walls resisting the vertical and lateral loads. The relative share of the lateral load resisted between these systems is dependent on their relative lateral stiffnesses. E-3.12.4 Structural Wall System with Flat Slab Floor System — A structural system comprising structural walls, a beam-less floor system, and columns resisting the vertical and lateral loads. The relative share of the lateral load resisted between these systems is dependent on their relative lateral stiffnesses. E-3.12.5 Core and Outrigger Structural System — A structural system comprising wall element(s) and perimeter columns, resisting the vertical and lateral loads. Essentially, the perimeter columns are for resisting gravity loads only. The core structure is connected to select perimeter column element(s) (often termed outrigger columns) by beam elements, known as outriggers, at discrete floor locations along the height of the building. This type of structure is an extension of the core structure, to enhance the lateral stiffness for taller structures, which mobilizes the perimeter columns, and offers increased leverage for push pull-action through the framing action offered by the deep beam(s) connecting the core to the outrigger columns. The global lateral stiffness is sensitive to: flexural stiffness of the core element, the flexural stiffness of the outrigger element(s) and the axial stiffness of the outrigger column(s).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
E-3.12.6 Core, Outrigger and Belt Wall System — A structural system, which is an extension to the core and outrigger structure to enhance the lateral stiffness further, where the outrigger column(s) is linked to the adjacent columns by deep beam elements (often known as belt truss), typically at the same level as the outrigger elements. The sharing of loads between multiple columns has the dual function of enhancing the axial stiffness and mobilizing greater number of gravity columns to counteract the induced tension loads generated by the overall lateral loads. PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 5 STRUCTURAL CONCRETE
E-3.12.7 Framed-Tube System — A structural system comprising closely spaced columns and deep beams in the perimeter frame for efficient tube action. The internal vertical elements, comprising core or columns are primarily utilized to resist gravity loads only. Effective utilization of the perimeter of the building maximizes the overall stiffness for a given building plan shape; this system is effective for very tall buildings. E-3.12.8 Tube-in-Tube System — A structural system, which is an extension of the tube structure, where there is an internal tube, often a core element, supplementing the external perimeter described as the tube structure above, to enhance the overall lateral global stiffness. Just as the tube structure, typically, even this system is suited for very tall buildings. E-3.12.9 Multiple-Tube System — A structural system, which is an extension of the tube structure and/or the tubein-tube structure, where the architectural plan of the tower facilitates multiple tubes to be connected together, to enhance the lateral stiffness of the structure. Just as the tube structure and the tube-in-tube structure, typically, this suited is reserved for very tall buildings. E-3.13 Super Tall Building — A building of height greater than 250 m. E-3.14 Tall Building — A building of height greater than 50 m, but less than or equal to 250 m.

Alternatively, it can be a trussed structure that fulfils the task through axial actions in the truss members. E-5.3 Storey Stiffness and Strength Parameters influencing stiffness and strength of the building should be so proportioned, that the following are maintained:
a) Lateral stiffness of any storey shall not be less than 70 percent of that of the storey above; and b) Lateral strength of any storey shall not be less than 90 percent that of the storey above. E-5.4  Deformations E-5.4.1 Lateral Drift When design lateral forces are applied on the building, the maximum inter-storey lateral drift ratio (Δmax/hi) under serviceability loads (including wind load with return period of 20 years), which is estimated based on the sectional properties for serviceability loads mentioned in E-7.2, shall be limited to 1/500. Total drift at the topmost usable floor shall be limited to H/500. For a single storey the drift limit may be relaxed to hi/400. E-5.5 Natural Modes of Vibration E-5.5.1 The natural period of fundamental torsional mode of vibration shall not exceed 0.9 times the smaller of the natural periods of the fundamental translational modes of vibration in each of the orthogonal directions in plan. E-5.6.2 Openings E-5.6.2.1 Openings in floor diaphragm shall not be permitted along any floor diaphragm edge, unless perimeter members are shown to have stability and adequate strength. E-5.6.2.2 The maximum area of openings in any floor diaphragm shall not exceed 30 percent of the plan area of diaphragm. E-5.6.2.3 At any storey, the minimum width of floor slab along any section after deduction of openings shall not be less than 5 m, if there is no perimeter beam. Further, the cumulative width of the slab at any location shall preferably not be less than 50 percent of the floor width. E-5.6.3 Natural Frequency of Floor System The natural vertical vibration frequency of any floor system shall not be less than 3 Hz without demonstration of acceptability using rational procedures. E-8.4.3 Special Requirements for Seismic Zone IV and above Special moment frame and shear walls shall not be discontinued in lower storeys and supported on less stiff and brittle elements. E-8.5 Structural Wall Systems E-8.5.1 The thickness of structural wall shall not be less than 160 mm or hi/20, whichever is larger. E-8.5.2 Opening in structural walls and the associated coupling beams shall meet the following requirements:
a) For walls, when the opening size is less than 800 mm or one-third length of wall, whichever is lesser, in height or length, the influence of the opening may not be taken into account in the overall stiffness of the building;
b) For beams, the opening size shall be less than one-third of the height or length of beam and location of the opening shall be such that the top and bottom one-third of height of the coupling beam is not disturbed; and c) In either case, all four sides of the opening shall be strengthened with additional reinforcements, and shall comply with requirements of good practice [C-5(5)]. Diameter of reinforcement bars used in this reinforcement shall not be less than 12 mm. E-8.5.3 Gravity columns in structural wall buildings shall be designed as per requirements of deformation compatibility on non-seismic members given in 5 of Part C/Section 1 of this NBCS. E-8.5.4 Beams carrying predominant vertical load shall not be supported on coupling beams. Also, columns or structural walls carrying predominant vertical load shall not be supported on coupling beam. E-8.5.5 In a structural wall system, the structural wall shall comply with the requirements of good practice [C-5(5)].

E-8.7  Framed Tube System, Tube-in-Tube System and Multiple Tube System E-8.7.1  The plan shape of a tube-in-tube system shall be regular with a length to width ratio not more than 2 and, the inner tube shall be centered with the outer tube. PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 5 STRUCTURAL CONCRETE (Clause E-8.5.11)
E-8.7.2  Reentrant corners and sharp changes to tubular form should be avoided. E-8.7.3  Column spacing of framed tube shall preferably be not more than 5 m. E-8.7.4  In a framed-tube system:
a) Area of corner column shall be 1 to 2 times that of internal column; and b) Height to width ratio of the opening shall be similar to ratio of storey height to column spacing. E-8.7.5 Due consideration shall be given to shear lag effects in the design of tube structures. E-8.7.6 In Seismic Zones III and above:
a) Single span frame shall not be adopted; and b) Axial compression ratio of columns shall be as per good practice [C-5(5)]. E-8.7.7 Beams carrying predominantly gravity load shall be directly supported on columns or on walls and not on frame beams. E-9.8  Settlements of Foundations Maximum vertical settlement of raft or piled raft foundations under gravity loads shall comply with requirements of good practice [C-5(40)] and good practice [C-5(41)]. The maximum vertical settlement is limited to 125 mm in raft or raft-pile foundation subject to maximum angular distortion of raft not exceeding 1/500 and 50 mm in rock. E-10 RECOMMENDATIONS FOR NON-STRUCTURAL ELEMENTS The non-structural elements (NSEs) of tall buildings shall comply with all relevant existing national standards and guidelines as laid down by the various statutory and non-statutory bodies as well as the client/owner of the building. E-11 MONITORING DEFORMATIONS IN BUILDINGS E-11.1 Earthquake Shaking All tall buildings in Seismic Zone V and tall buildings exceeding 150 m in Seismic Zone III and IV shall be instrumented with tri-axial accelerometers to capture translational and twisting behavior of buildings during strong earthquake shaking. E-11.2 Wind Oscillations Buildings over 150 m in height may be instrumented with anemometers and accelerometers to measure wind speed, acceleration and direction on top of the buildings. PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 5 STRUCTURAL CONCRETE
E-11.3.1 Permanent settlement markers (at corners and center) shall be provided at raft top level and referenced to a permanent benchmark. Records of settlement shall be maintained till completion of the building and preferably even after completion. E-11.3.2 Raft or Piled-raft shall be instrumented for monitoring long-term pressure imposed by soil on the raft, at appropriate number (at least 5) of pressure pads below the raft. Alternatively, piles can be instrumented with strain gauges at their top to measure the load on them. National Building Code Sectional Committee, CED 46 FOREWORD This NBCS (Part C/Subsection 6A) covers the structural design aspects of steel structures in buildings. This Section covers the use of hot-rolled structural steel sections and steel tubes in buildings. It covers the design by limit state method and plastic theory. This Section was first published in 1970 and revised in 1983, 2005 and 2016 as a chapter of the National Building Code of India. In the second revision of 2005, the detailed design provisions were not included as IS 800 : 1984 ‘Code of practice for general construction in steel (second revision)’ was under revision at that time. This Section, therefore, then referred to the 1984 version of IS 800 with the remarks that the latest version would prevail, as and when published. It, however, covered the philosophical aspects of limit state design which was being introduced in the revision of IS 800.

In the 2016 version of the Code, this Section was brought it in line with the revised version of IS 800 : 2007 read with its Amendment No. 1 and to take care of further improvements and incorporations required. In the current revision, this publication has been renamed as National Building Construction Standards (NBCS). This revision of the Section is intended to bring it in line with the revised version of IS 800 : 2026 (under publication) to take care of further improvements and incorporations required.

chunks.section_title: This NBCS (Part C/Subsection 6A) covers the structural design aspects of steel structures in buildings. This
chunks.text:
1.1 This NBCS (Part C/Subsection 6A) covers the structural design aspects of steel structures in buildings. This
Section applies to general construction using hot rolled steel sections and steel tubes joined using riveting, bolting, and welding.  Cold formed light gauge steel sections are covered in separate standards. This Section covers the design by limit state method and plastic theory.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: This Section gives only general guidance as regards to the various loads to be considered in the design. For
chunks.text:
1.2 This Section gives only general guidance as regards to the various loads to be considered in the design. For
the actual loads, such as dead, imposed, snow, wind and earthquake loads and load combinations to be used, reference may be made to Part C ‘Structural Design/Section 1 Loads and Load Effects’ of this NBCS.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fabrication and erection requirements covered in this Section are general and the minimum necessary quality
chunks.text:
1.3 Fabrication and erection requirements covered in this Section are general and the minimum necessary quality
of material and workmanship consistent with assumptions in the design rules. The actual requirements may be further developed as per other standards or the project specification, the type of structure and the method of construction.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: For seismic design, recommendations pertaining to steel frames only are covered in this section. For more
chunks.text:
1.4 For seismic design, recommendations pertaining to steel frames only are covered in this section. For more
detailed information on seismic design of other structural and non-structural components, reference be made to 5 of Part C ‘Structural Design/Section 1 Loads and Load Effects’ of this NBCS and other special publications on the subject.

chunks.text:

chunks.text:

chunks.text:

chunks.section_title: Cumulative Fatigue — Total damage due to fatigue loading of varying stress ranges.
chunks.text: 3.21 Cumulative Fatigue — Total damage due to fatigue loading of varying stress ranges.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Cut-off Limit — The stress range, corresponding to the particular detail, below which cyclic loading need
chunks.text:
3.22 Cut-off Limit — The stress range, corresponding to the particular detail, below which cyclic loading need
not be considered in cumulative fatigue damage evaluation (corresponds to 108 number of cycles in most cases).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Dead Loads — The self-weights of all permanent constructions and installations including the self-weight
chunks.text:
3.23 Dead Loads — The self-weights of all permanent constructions and installations including the self-weight
of all walls, partitions, floors, roofs, and other permanent fixtures acting on a member.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Deflection — The deviation from the standard position of a member or structure.
chunks.text: 3.24 Deflection — The deviation from the standard position of a member or structure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Design Life — Time period for which a structure or a structural element is required to perform its function
chunks.text:
3.25 Design Life — Time period for which a structure or a structural element is required to perform its function
without damage.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Design Load/Factored Load — A load value obtained by multiplying the characteristic load with the partial
chunks.text:
3.26 Design Load/Factored Load — A load value obtained by multiplying the characteristic load with the partial
safety factor for loads.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Design Spectrum — Frequency distribution of the stress ranges from all the nominal loading events during
chunks.text:
3.27 Design Spectrum — Frequency distribution of the stress ranges from all the nominal loading events during
the design life (stress spectrum).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Detail Category — Designation given to a particular detail to indicate the S-N curve to be used in fatigue
chunks.text:
3.28 Detail Category — Designation given to a particular detail to indicate the S-N curve to be used in fatigue
assessment.
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Discontinuity — A sudden change in cross section of a loaded member, causing a stress concentration at the
chunks.text:
3.29 Discontinuity — A sudden change in cross section of a loaded member, causing a stress concentration at the
location.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Ductility — The property of the material or a structure indicating the extent to which it can deform beyond
chunks.text:
3.30 Ductility — The property of the material or a structure indicating the extent to which it can deform beyond
the limit of yield deformation before failure or fracture.  The ratio of ultimate to yield deformation is usually termed as ductility.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Durability — The ability of a material to resist deterioration over long periods of time.
chunks.text: 3.31 Durability — The ability of a material to resist deterioration over long periods of time.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Earthquake effects — The inertia forces and relative deformations induced in a structure due to the ground
chunks.text:
3.32 Earthquake effects — The inertia forces and relative deformations induced in a structure due to the ground
shaking during an earthquake.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Edge Distance — Distance from the centre of a fastener hole to the nearest edge of an element measured
chunks.text:
3.33 Edge Distance — Distance from the centre of a fastener hole to the nearest edge of an element measured
perpendicular to the direction of load transfer.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Effective Lateral Restraint — Restraint that produces sufficient resistance to prevent deformation in the
chunks.text:
3.34 Effective Lateral Restraint — Restraint that produces sufficient resistance to prevent deformation in the
lateral direction.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Effective Length — Actual length of a member between points of effective restraint or effective restraint
chunks.text:
3.35 Effective Length — Actual length of a member between points of effective restraint or effective restraint
and free end, multiplied by a factor to take account of the end conditions in buckling strength calculations.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Elastic Cladding — Claddings, such as metal sheets that can undergo considerable deformation without
chunks.text:
3.36 Elastic Cladding — Claddings, such as metal sheets that can undergo considerable deformation without
damage.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Elastic Critical Moment — The elastic moment, which initiates lateral-torsional buckling of a laterally
chunks.text:
3.37 Elastic Critical Moment — The elastic moment, which initiates lateral-torsional buckling of a laterally
unsupported beam.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Elastic Design — Design, which assumes elastic behaviour of materials throughout the service load range.
chunks.text: 3.38 Elastic Design — Design, which assumes elastic behaviour of materials throughout the service load range.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Elastic Limit — The stress below which the material regains its original size and shape when the load is
chunks.text:
3.39 Elastic Limit — The stress below which the material regains its original size and shape when the load is
removed. In steel design, it is taken as the yield stress.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: End Distance — Distance from the centre of a fastener hole to the edge of an element measured parallel to
chunks.text:
3.40 End Distance — Distance from the centre of a fastener hole to the edge of an element measured parallel to
the direction of load transfer.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Erection Loads — The actions (loads and deformations) experienced by the structure exclusively during
chunks.text:
3.41 Erection Loads — The actions (loads and deformations) experienced by the structure exclusively during
erection.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Erection Tolerance — Amount of deviation related to the plumbness, alignment, and level of the element
chunks.text:
3.42 Erection Tolerance — Amount of deviation related to the plumbness, alignment, and level of the element
as a whole in the erected position.  The deviations are determined by considering the locations of the ends of the element.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Exposed Surface Area to Mass Ratio — The ratio of the surface area exposed to the fire (in mm2) to the
chunks.text:
3.43 Exposed Surface Area to Mass Ratio — The ratio of the surface area exposed to the fire (in mm2) to the
mass of steel (in kg).
NOTE — In the case of members with fire protection material applied, the exposed surface area is to be taken as the internal surface area of the fire protection material.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fabrication Tolerance — Amount of deviation allowed in the nominal dimensions and geometry in
chunks.text:
3.44 Fabrication Tolerance — Amount of deviation allowed in the nominal dimensions and geometry in
fabrication activities, such as cutting to length, finishing of ends, cutting of bevel angles, etc.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Factor of Safety — The factor by which the yield stress of the material of a member is divided to arrive at
chunks.text:
3.45 Factor of Safety — The factor by which the yield stress of the material of a member is divided to arrive at
the permissible stress in the material.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fatigue — Damage caused by repeated fluctuations of stress, leading to progressive cracking of a structural
chunks.text:
3.46 Fatigue — Damage caused by repeated fluctuations of stress, leading to progressive cracking of a structural
element.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fatigue Loading — Set of nominal loading events, cyclic in nature, described by the distribution of the
chunks.text:
3.47 Fatigue Loading — Set of nominal loading events, cyclic in nature, described by the distribution of the
loads, their magnitudes and the numbers of applications in each nominal loading event.
PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 6 STEEL AND COMPOSITE CONSTRUCTION: 6(A) STEEL
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fatigue Strength — The stress range for a category of detail, depending upon the number of cycles it is
chunks.text:
3.48 Fatigue Strength — The stress range for a category of detail, depending upon the number of cycles it is
required to withstand during design life.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 3.49 Fire Exposure Condition
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Three-Sided Fire Exposure Condition — Steel member incorporated in or in contact with a concrete or
chunks.text:
3.49.1 Three-Sided Fire Exposure Condition — Steel member incorporated in or in contact with a concrete or
masonry floor or wall (at least against on surface); and NOTES
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Three-sided fire exposure condition is to be considered separately unless otherwise specified (see 22.9).
chunks.text: 1 Three-sided fire exposure condition is to be considered separately unless otherwise specified (see 22.9).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Members with more than one face in contact with a concrete or masonry floor or wall may be treated as three-sided fire exposure.
chunks.text: 2 Members with more than one face in contact with a concrete or masonry floor or wall may be treated as three-sided fire exposure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Four-Sided Fire Exposure Condition — Steel member, which may be exposed to fire on all sides.
chunks.text: 3.49.2 Four-Sided Fire Exposure Condition — Steel member, which may be exposed to fire on all sides.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fire Protection System — The fire protection material and its method of attachment to the steel member.
chunks.text: 3.50 Fire Protection System — The fire protection material and its method of attachment to the steel member.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fire Resistance — The ability of an element, component or structure, to fulfil for a stated period of time,
chunks.text:
3.51 Fire Resistance — The ability of an element, component or structure, to fulfil for a stated period of time,
the required stability, integrity, thermal insulation and/or other expected performance specified in a standard fire test.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Fire Resistance Level — The fire resistance grading period for a structural element or system, in minutes,
chunks.text:
3.52 Fire Resistance Level — The fire resistance grading period for a structural element or system, in minutes,
which is required to be attained in the standard fire test.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Flexural Stiffness — Stiffness of a member against rotation as evaluated by the value of bending
chunks.text:
3.53 Flexural Stiffness — Stiffness of a member against rotation as evaluated by the value of bending
deformation moment required to cause a unit rotation while all other degrees of freedom of the joints of the member except the rotated one are assumed to be restrained.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Friction Type Connection — Connection effected by using pre-tensioned high strength bolts where shear
chunks.text:
3.54 Friction Type Connection — Connection effected by using pre-tensioned high strength bolts where shear
force transfer is due to mobilization of friction between the connected plates due to clamping force developed at the interface of connected plates by the bolt pre-tension.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Gauge — The spacing between adjacent parallel lines of fasteners, transverse to the direction of load/stress.
chunks.text: 3.55 Gauge — The spacing between adjacent parallel lines of fasteners, transverse to the direction of load/stress.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Gravity Load — Loads arising due to gravitational effects.
chunks.text: 3.56 Gravity Load — Loads arising due to gravitational effects.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Gusset Plate — The plate to which the members intersecting at a joint are connected.
chunks.text: 3.57 Gusset Plate — The plate to which the members intersecting at a joint are connected.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: High Shear — High shear condition is caused when the actual shear due to factored load is greater than a
chunks.text:
3.58 High Shear — High shear condition is caused when the actual shear due to factored load is greater than a
certain fraction of design shear resistance (see 16.2.2).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Imposed (Live) Load — The load assumed to be produced by the intended use or occupancy including
chunks.text:
3.59 Imposed (Live) Load — The load assumed to be produced by the intended use or occupancy including
distributed, concentrated, impact, vibration and snow loads but excluding, wind, earthquake and temperature effects.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Instability — The phenomenon which disables an element, member or a structure to carry further load due
chunks.text:
3.60 Instability — The phenomenon which disables an element, member or a structure to carry further load due
to excessive deflection lateral to the direction of loading and vanishing stiffness.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Lateral Restraint for a Beam — See 3.34.
chunks.text: 3.61 Lateral Restraint for a Beam — See 3.34.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Leading Imposed Load — Imposed load causing higher action and/or deflection.
chunks.text: 3.62 Leading Imposed Load — Imposed load causing higher action and/or deflection.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Limit State — Any limiting condition beyond which the structure ceases to fulfill its intended function
chunks.text:
3.63 Limit State — Any limiting condition beyond which the structure ceases to fulfill its intended function
(see also 3.86).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 3.64 Live Load — See 3.59.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Load — An externally applied force or action (see also 3.4).
chunks.text: 3.65 Load — An externally applied force or action (see also 3.4).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Main Member — A structural member, which is primarily responsible for carrying and distributing the
chunks.text:
3.66 Main Member — A structural member, which is primarily responsible for carrying and distributing the
applied load or action.
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Mill Tolerance — Amount of variation allowed from the nominal dimensions and geometry, with respect to
chunks.text:
3.67 Mill Tolerance — Amount of variation allowed from the nominal dimensions and geometry, with respect to
cross sectional area, non-parallelism of flanges, and out of straightness such as sweep or camber, in a product, as manufactured in a steel mill.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Normal Stress — Stress component acting normal to the face, plane or section.
chunks.text: 3.68 Normal Stress — Stress component acting normal to the face, plane or section.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Partial Safety Factor — The factor normally greater than unity by which either the loads (actions) are
chunks.text:
3.69 Partial Safety Factor — The factor normally greater than unity by which either the loads (actions) are
multiplied or the resistances are divided to obtain the design values.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Period of Structural Adequacy under Fire — The time (t), in minutes, for the member to reach the limit
chunks.text:
3.70 Period of Structural Adequacy under Fire — The time (t), in minutes, for the member to reach the limit
state of structural inadequacy in a standard fire test.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Permissible Stress — When a structure is being designed by the working stress method, the maximum stress
chunks.text:
3.71 Permissible Stress — When a structure is being designed by the working stress method, the maximum stress
that is permitted to be experienced in elements, members or structures under the nominal/service load (action).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Pitch — The centre to centre distance between individual fasteners in a line, in the direction of load/stress.
chunks.text: 3.72 Pitch — The centre to centre distance between individual fasteners in a line, in the direction of load/stress.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Plastic Collapse — The failure stage at which sufficient number of plastic hinges have formed due to the
chunks.text:
3.73 Plastic Collapse — The failure stage at which sufficient number of plastic hinges have formed due to the
loads (actions) in a structure leading to a failure mechanism.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Plastic Design — Design against the limit state of plastic collapse.
chunks.text: 3.74 Plastic Design — Design against the limit state of plastic collapse.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Plastic Hinge — A yielding zone with significant inelastic rotation, which forms in a member, when the
chunks.text:
3.75 Plastic Hinge — A yielding zone with significant inelastic rotation, which forms in a member, when the
plastic moment is reached at a section.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Plastic Moment — Moment capacity of a cross section when the entire cross section has yielded due to
chunks.text:
3.76 Plastic Moment — Moment capacity of a cross section when the entire cross section has yielded due to
bending moment.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Plastic Section — Cross section, which can develop a plastic hinge and sustain plastic moment over
chunks.text:
3.77 Plastic Section — Cross section, which can develop a plastic hinge and sustain plastic moment over
sufficient plastic rotation required for formation of plastic failure mechanism of the member or structure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Poisson’s Ratio — The absolute value of the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain under uniaxial
chunks.text:
3.78 Poisson’s Ratio — The absolute value of the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain under uniaxial
loading.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Proof Stress — The stress to which high strength friction grip (HSFG) bolts are pre-tensioned.
chunks.text: 3.79 Proof Stress — The stress to which high strength friction grip (HSFG) bolts are pre-tensioned.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Proof Testing — The application of test loads to a structure, sub-structure, member or connection to ascertain
chunks.text:
3.80 Proof Testing — The application of test loads to a structure, sub-structure, member or connection to ascertain
the structural characteristics of only that specific unit.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Prototype Testing — Testing of structure, sub-structure, members or connections to ascertain the structural
chunks.text:
3.81 Prototype Testing — Testing of structure, sub-structure, members or connections to ascertain the structural
characteristics of that class of structures, sub-structures, members or connections that are nominally identical (full scale) to the units tested.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Prying Force — Additional tensile force developed in a bolt as a result of the flexing of a connection
chunks.text:
3.82 Prying Force — Additional tensile force developed in a bolt as a result of the flexing of a connection
component such as a beam end plate or leg of an angle.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Rotation — The change in angle at a joint between the original orientation of two linear member and their
chunks.text:
3.83 Rotation — The change in angle at a joint between the original orientation of two linear member and their
final position under loading.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Secondary Member — Member which is provided for overall stability and or for restraining the main
chunks.text:
3.84 Secondary Member — Member which is provided for overall stability and or for restraining the main
members from buckling or similar modes of failure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Semi-compact Section — Cross section, which can attain the yield moment, but not the plastic moment
chunks.text:
3.85 Semi-compact Section — Cross section, which can attain the yield moment, but not the plastic moment
before failure by plate buckling.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Serviceability Limit State — A limit state of acceptable service condition exceedance of which causes
chunks.text:
3.86 Serviceability Limit State — A limit state of acceptable service condition exceedance of which causes
serviceability failure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Shear Force — The in-plane force at any transverse cross section of a straight member of a column or beam.
chunks.text:
3.87 Shear Force — The in-plane force at any transverse cross section of a straight member of a column or beam.
PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 6 STEEL AND COMPOSITE CONSTRUCTION: 6(A) STEEL
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Shear lag — The in plane shear deformation effect by which concentrated forces tangential to the surface of
chunks.text:
3.88 Shear lag — The in plane shear deformation effect by which concentrated forces tangential to the surface of
a plate gets distributed over the entire section perpendicular to the load over a finite length of the plate along the direction of the load.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Shear Stress — The stress component acting parallel to a face, plane or cross section.
chunks.text: 3.89 Shear Stress — The stress component acting parallel to a face, plane or cross section.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Slender Section — Cross section in which the elements buckle locally before reaching yield moment.
chunks.text: 3.90 Slender Section — Cross section in which the elements buckle locally before reaching yield moment.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Slenderness Ratio — The ratio of the effective length of a member to the radius of gyration of the cross
chunks.text:
3.91 Slenderness Ratio — The ratio of the effective length of a member to the radius of gyration of the cross
section about the axis under consideration.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Slip Resistance — Limit shear that can be applied in a friction grip connection before slip occurs.
chunks.text: 3.92 Slip Resistance — Limit shear that can be applied in a friction grip connection before slip occurs.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: S-N Curve — The curve defining the relationship between the number of stress cycles to failure (Nsc) at a
chunks.text:
3.93 S-N Curve — The curve defining the relationship between the number of stress cycles to failure (Nsc) at a
constant stress range (Sc), during fatigue loading of a structure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Snow Load — Load on a structure due to the accumulation of snow and ice on surfaces such as roof.
chunks.text: 3.94 Snow Load — Load on a structure due to the accumulation of snow and ice on surfaces such as roof.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Snug Tight — The tightness of a bolt achieved by a few impacts of an impact wrench or by the full effort of
chunks.text:
3.95 Snug Tight — The tightness of a bolt achieved by a few impacts of an impact wrench or by the full effort of
a person using a standard spanner.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stability Limit State — A limit state corresponding to the loss of static equilibrium of a structure by
chunks.text:
3.96 Stability Limit State — A limit state corresponding to the loss of static equilibrium of a structure by
excessive deflection transverse to the direction of predominant loads.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stickability — The ability of the fire protection system to remain in place as the member deflects under load
chunks.text:
3.97 Stickability — The ability of the fire protection system to remain in place as the member deflects under load
during a fire test.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stiffener — An element used to retain or prevent the out-of-plane deformations of plates.
chunks.text: 3.98 Stiffener — An element used to retain or prevent the out-of-plane deformations of plates.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Strain — Deformation per unit length or unit angle.
chunks.text: 3.99 Strain — Deformation per unit length or unit angle.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Strain Hardening — The phenomenon of increase in stress with increase in strain beyond yielding.
chunks.text: 3.100 Strain Hardening — The phenomenon of increase in stress with increase in strain beyond yielding.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Strength — Resistance to failure by yielding or buckling.
chunks.text: 3.101 Strength — Resistance to failure by yielding or buckling.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Strength Limit State — A limit state of collapse or loss of structural integrity.
chunks.text: 3.102 Strength Limit State — A limit state of collapse or loss of structural integrity.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stress — The internal force per unit area of the original cross section.
chunks.text: 3.103 Stress — The internal force per unit area of the original cross section.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stress Analysis — The analysis of the internal force and stress condition in an element, member or
chunks.text:
3.104 Stress Analysis — The analysis of the internal force and stress condition in an element, member or
structure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stress Cycle Counting — Sum of individual stress cycles from stress history arrived at using any rational
chunks.text:
3.105 Stress Cycle Counting — Sum of individual stress cycles from stress history arrived at using any rational
method.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stress Range — Algebraic difference between two extremes of stresses in a cycle of loading.
chunks.text: 3.106 Stress Range — Algebraic difference between two extremes of stresses in a cycle of loading.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Stress Spectrum — Histogram of stress cycles produced by a nominal loading event design spectrum,
chunks.text:
3.107 Stress Spectrum — Histogram of stress cycles produced by a nominal loading event design spectrum,
during design life.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Structural Adequacy for Fire — The ability of the member to carry the test load exposed to the standard
chunks.text:
3.108 Structural Adequacy for Fire — The ability of the member to carry the test load exposed to the standard
fire test.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Structural Analysis — The analysis of stress, strain, and deflection characteristics of a structure.
chunks.text: 3.109 Structural Analysis — The analysis of stress, strain, and deflection characteristics of a structure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Strut — A compression member, which may be oriented in any direction.

6 STANDARD DIMENSIONS, FORM AND WEIGHT

chunks.text: 7 PLANS AND DRAWINGS
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Plans, drawings and stress sheet shall be prepared according to accepted standards [C-6A(3)].
chunks.text: 7.1 Plans, drawings and stress sheet shall be prepared according to accepted standards [C-6A(3)].
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
7.1.1 Plans
The plans (design drawings) shall show the sizes, sections, and the relative locations of the various members.
Floor levels, column centres, and offsets shall be dimensioned.  Plans shall be drawn to a scale large enough to convey the information adequately. Plans shall indicate the type of construction to be employed; and shall be supplemented by such data on the assumed loads, shears, moments and axial forces to be resisted by all members and their connections, as may be required for the proper preparation of shop drawings.  Any special precaution to be taken in the erection of structure, from the design consideration shall also be indicated in the drawing.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
7.1.2 Shop Drawings
Shop drawings, giving complete information necessary for the fabrication of the component parts of the structure including the location, type, size, length and detail of all welds and fasteners shall be prepared in advance of the actual fabrication.  They shall clearly distinguish between shop and field rivets, bolts and welds. For additional information to be included on drawings for designs based on the use of welding, reference shall be made to appropriate Indian Standards.  Shop drawings shall be made in conformity with accepted standard [C-6A(4)].
A marking diagram allotting distinct identification marks to each separate part of steel work shall be prepared.
The diagram shall be sufficient to ensure convenient assembly and erection at site.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

8 CONVENTION FOR MEMBER AXES
Unless otherwise specified convention used for member axes is as follows (Fig. 1):
a) x-x along the member;
b) y-y an axis of the cross section:
1) perpendicular to the flanges; and 2) perpendicular to the smaller leg in an angle section.
c) z-z an axis of the cross-section:

1) axis parallel to flanges; and 2) axis parallel to smaller leg in angle section.
d) u-u major axis (when it does not coincide with z-z axis); and e) v-v minor axis (when it does not coincide with y-y axis).

chunks.text: 10 GENERAL DESIGN REQUIREMENTS
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 10.1 Basis for Design
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
10.1.1 Design Objective
The objective of design is the achievement of an acceptable probability that structures will perform satisfactorily for the intended purpose during the design life. With an appropriate degree of safety, they should sustain all the loads and deformations, during construction and use and have adequate resistance to certain expected accidental loads and fire. Structure should be stable and have alternate load paths to prevent disproportionate overall collapse under accidental loading.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
10.1.2 Methods of Design
Structure and its elements shall normally, be designed by the limit state method. Account should be taken of accepted theories, experimental information and experience and the need to design for durability. Calculations alone may not produce safe, serviceable and durable structures. Suitable materials, quality control, adequate detailing and good supervision are equally important.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
10.1.3 Design Process
Structural design, including design for durability, construction and use should be considered as a whole.  The realization of design objectives requires compliance with clearly defined standards for materials, fabrication, erection and in-service maintenance.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The fire loads, erection loads and temperature effects shall be considered as specified in 10.3, 10.4
chunks.text:
10.2.1.5 The fire loads, erection loads and temperature effects shall be considered as specified in 10.3, 10.4
and 10.5, respectively.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
10.3 Fire Loads
During a fire, the structural members around the fire experience higher temperatures. This causes expansion in members that is restrained by rest of the structure, inducing forces in the members. Simultaneously, due to high temperature both strength and stiffness of the members experiencing the higher temperature degrade. The forces in members during fire including that due to dead load and imposed load are checked against the reduced capacity of the members. As it is an extreme event, the design is done for loads without extra partial safety factors. The imposed load is taken as 100 percent of the characteristic Imposed loads in case of storage areas and otherwise taken as 50 percent of the characteristic Imposed load value, during fire.
Due to proper fire protection, the temperature felt by the members may be less than the ambient temperature, and this may be taken into consideration in evaluating temperature effects due to fire.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
10.4 Erection Loads
All loads required to be carried by the structure or any part of it due to storage or positioning of construction material and erection equipment, including all loads due to operation of such equipment shall be considered as erection loads.  Proper provision shall be made, including temporary bracings, to take care of all stresses developed during erection.  Dead load, wind load and also such parts of the imposed load as would be imposed on the structure during the period of erection shall be taken as acting together with the erection loads.  The structure as a whole and all parts of the structure in conjunction with the temporary bracings shall be capable of sustaining these loads during erection.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 10.5 Temperature Effects
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Expansion and contraction due to changes in temperature of the members and elements of a structure shall
chunks.text:
10.5.1 Expansion and contraction due to changes in temperature of the members and elements of a structure shall
be considered and adequate provision made for such effect.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The temperature range varies for different localities and under different diurnal and seasonal conditions.
chunks.text:
10.5.2 The temperature range varies for different localities and under different diurnal and seasonal conditions.
The absolute maximum and minimum temperatures, which may be expected at the site, may be obtained from the Indian Metrological Department and used in assessing the maximum variations of temperature for which provision for expansion and contraction has to be made in the structure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The range of variation in temperature of the building materials may be appreciably greater or lesser than
chunks.text:
10.5.3 The range of variation in temperature of the building materials may be appreciably greater or lesser than
the variation of air temperature and is influenced by the condition of exposure and the rate at which the materials composing the structure absorb or radiate heat.  This difference in temperature variations of the material and air shall be given due consideration.  The effect of differential temperature within an element or member, due to part exposure to direct sunlight shall also be considered.

chunks.section_title: The coefficient of thermal expansion for steel is as given in 9.2.4.1(e).

chunks.text: 10.7 Geometrical Properties
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
10.7.1 General
The geometrical properties of the gross and the effective cross sections of a member or part thereof, shall be calculated on the following basis:
a) the properties of the gross cross section shall be calculated from the specified size of the member or part thereof or read from appropriate table; and b) the properties of the effective cross section shall be calculated by deducting from the area of the gross cross section, in the following:
1) The sectional area in excess of effective plate width, in case of slender sections [see 10.8.2 (d)]; and 2) The sectional areas of all holes in the section except for parts in compression.  In case of punched holes, hole size 2 mm in excess of the actual diameter may be deducted.

10.8.3 Types of Elements
a) Internal elements — These are elements attached along both longitudinal edges to other elements or to longitudinal stiffeners connected at suitable intervals to transverse stiffeners; for example, web of I-section and flanges and web of box section;
b) Outside elements or outstands — These are elements attached along only one of the longitudinal edges to an adjacent element, the other edge being free to displace out of plane, for example flange overhang of an I-section, stem of T-section and legs of an angle section; and c) Tapered elements — These may be treated as flat elements having average thickness as defined in accepted standard [C-6A(36)].
The design of slender compression element (Class 4) considering the strength beyond elastic local buckling of element is outside the scope of this section.  Reference may be made to in good practice [C-6A(35)] for such design provisions.  The design of slender web elements may be made as given in 15.2.1.1 for flexure and 15.4.2.2 for shear.
