chunks.text: 17 CONNECTIONS
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 17.1 General
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: This Section deals with the design and detailing requirements for joints between members. Connection
chunks.text:
17.1.1 This Section deals with the design and detailing requirements for joints between members. Connection
elements consist of components such as cleats, gusset plates, brackets, connecting plates and connectors such as rivets, bolts, pins, and welds. The connections in a structure shall be designed so as to be consistent with the assumptions made in the analysis of the structure and comply with the requirements specified in this section.
Connections shall be capable of transmitting the calculated design actions.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Where members are connected to the surface of a web or the flange of a section, the ability of the web or
chunks.text:
17.1.2  Where members are connected to the surface of a web or the flange of a section, the ability of the web or
the flange to transfer the applied forces locally should be checked and where necessary, local stiffening provided.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Ease of fabrication and erection should be considered in the design of connections. Attention should be
chunks.text:
17.1.3 Ease of fabrication and erection should be considered in the design of connections. Attention should be
paid to clearances necessary for field erection, tolerances, tightening of fasteners, welding procedures, subsequent inspection, surface treatment and maintenance.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The ductility of steel assists the distribution of forces generated within a joint. Effects of residual stresses
chunks.text:
17.1.4  The ductility of steel assists the distribution of forces generated within a joint. Effects of residual stresses
and stresses due to tightening of fasteners and normal tolerances of fit-up need not therefore be considered in connection design, provided ductile behaviour is ensured.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: In general, use of different forms of fasteners to transfer the same force shall be avoided. However, when
chunks.text:
17.1.5  In general, use of different forms of fasteners to transfer the same force shall be avoided. However, when
different forms of fasteners are used to carry a shear load or when welding and fasteners are combined, then one form of fastener shall be normally designed to carry the total load. Nevertheless, fully tensioned friction grip bolts may be designed to share the load with welding, provided the bolts are fully tightened to develop necessary pretension after welding.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The partial safety factor in the evaluation of design strength of connections shall be taken as given in
chunks.text:
17.1.6 The partial safety factor in the evaluation of design strength of connections shall be taken as given in
Table 5.

17.2.2 Minimum Spacing
The distance between centres of fasteners shall not be less than 2.5 times the nominal diameter of the fastener.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 17.2.3 Maximum Spacing
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The distance between the centres of any two adjacent fasteners shall not exceed 32t or 300 mm, whichever
chunks.text:
17.2.3.1 The distance between the centres of any two adjacent fasteners shall not exceed 32t or 300 mm, whichever
is less, where t is the thickness of the thinner plate.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The distance between the centres of two adjacent fasteners (pitch) in a line lying in the direction of stress,
chunks.text:
17.2.3.2 The distance between the centres of two adjacent fasteners (pitch) in a line lying in the direction of stress,
shall not exceed 16t or 200 mm, whichever is less, in tension members and 12t or 200 mm, whichever is less, in compression members; where t is the thickness of the thinner plate. In the case of compression members wherein forces are transferred through butting faces, this distance shall not exceed 4.5 times the diameter of the fasteners for a distance equal to 1.5 times the width of the member from the butting faces.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The distance between the centres of any two consecutive fasteners in a line adjacent and parallel to an
chunks.text:
17.2.3.3 The distance between the centres of any two consecutive fasteners in a line adjacent and parallel to an
edge of an outside plate shall not exceed 100 mm plus 4t or 200 mm, whichever is less, in compression and tension members; where t is the thickness of the thinner outside plate.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: When fasteners are staggered at equal intervals and the gauge does not exceed 75 mm, the spacing
chunks.text:
17.2.3.4 When fasteners are staggered at equal intervals and the gauge does not exceed 75 mm, the spacing
specified in 17.2.3.2 and 17.2.3.3 between centres of fasteners may be increased by 50 percent, subject to the maximum spacing specified in 17.2.3.1.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 17.2.4  Edge and End Distances
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The edge distance is the distance at right angles to the direction of stress from the centre of a hole to the
chunks.text:
17.2.4.1 The edge distance is the distance at right angles to the direction of stress from the centre of a hole to the
adjacent edge.  The end distance is the distance in the direction of stress from the centre of a hole to the end of the element.
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
In slotted holes, the edge and end distances should be measured from the edge or end of the material to the centre of its end radius or the centre line of the slot, whichever is smaller.  In oversize holes, the edge and end distances should be taken as the distance from the relevant edge/end plus half the diameter of the standard clearance hole corresponding to the fastener, less the nominal diameter of the oversize hole.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The minimum edge and end distances from the centre of any hole to the nearest edge of a plate shall not
chunks.text:
17.2.4.2 The minimum edge and end distances from the centre of any hole to the nearest edge of a plate shall not
be less than 1.7 times the hole diameter in case of sheared or hand-flame cut edges; and 1.5 times the hole diameter in case of rolled, machine-flame cut, sawn and planed edges.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The maximum edge distance to the nearest line of fasteners from an edge of any un-stiffened part should
chunks.text:
17.2.4.3 The maximum edge distance to the nearest line of fasteners from an edge of any un-stiffened part should
not exceed 12 t, where  = (250/fy)1/2 and t is the thickness of the thinner outer plate.  This would not apply to fasteners interconnecting the components of back to back tension members.  Where the members are exposed to corrosive influences, the maximum edge distance shall not exceed 40 mm plus 4t, where t is the thickness of thinner connected plate.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 17.2.5 Tacking Fasteners
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: In case of members covered under 17.2.4.3, when the maximum distance between centres of two adjacent
chunks.text:
17.2.5.1 In case of members covered under 17.2.4.3, when the maximum distance between centres of two adjacent
fasteners as specified in 17.2.4.3 is exceeded, tacking fasteners not subjected to calculated stress shall be used.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Tacking fasteners shall have spacing in a line not exceeding 32 times the thickness of the thinner outside
chunks.text:
17.2.5.2 Tacking fasteners shall have spacing in a line not exceeding 32 times the thickness of the thinner outside
plate or 300 mm, whichever is less. Where the plates are exposed to the weather, the spacing in line shall not exceed 16 times the thickness of the thinner outside plate or 200 mm, whichever is less.  In both cases, the distance between the lines of fasteners shall not be greater than the respective pitches.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: All the requirements specified in 17.2.5.2 shall generally apply to compression members, subject to the
chunks.text:
17.2.5.3 All the requirements specified in 17.2.5.2 shall generally apply to compression members, subject to the
stipulations given under 14 affecting the design and construction of compression members.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: In tension members [see 13] composed of two flats, angles, channels or tees in contact back to back or
chunks.text:
17.2.5.4 In tension members [see 13] composed of two flats, angles, channels or tees in contact back to back or
separated back to back by a distance not exceeding the aggregate thickness of the connected parts, tacking fasteners with solid distance pieces shall be provided at a spacing in line not exceeding 1 000 mm.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: For compression members covered under 14, tacking fasteners in a line shall be spaced at a distance not
chunks.text:

exceeding 600 mm.

17.5.1.1 End returns
Fillet welds terminating at the ends or sides of parts should be returned continuously around the corners for a distance of not less than twice the size of the weld, unless it is impractical to do so. This is particularly important on the tension end of parts carrying bending loads.

chunks.text:
17.5.1.2 Lap joint
In the case of lap joints, the minimum lap should not be less than four times the thickness of the thinner part joined or 40 mm, whichever is more. Single end fillet should be used only when lapped parts are restrained from openings. When end of an element is connected only by parallel longitudinal fillet welds, the length of the weld along either edge should not be less than the transverse spacing between longitudinal welds.

chunks.section_title: Connections can be classified as rigid, semi-rigid and flexible for the purpose of analysis and design as per
chunks.text:
17.6.1 Connections can be classified as rigid, semi-rigid and flexible for the purpose of analysis and design as per
the recommendation in Annex F. Connections with sufficient rotational stiffness may be considered as rigid.
Examples of rigid connections include flush end-plate connection and extended end-plate connections.
Connections with negligible rotational stiffness may be considered as flexible (pinned). Examples of flexible connections include single and double web angle connections and header plate connections. Where a connection cannot be classified as either rigid or flexible, it shall be assumed to be semi-rigid. 17.8 Intersections
Members or components meeting at a joint shall be arranged to transfer the design actions between the parts, wherever practicable, with their centroidal axes meeting at a point. chunks.text: 17.11 Analysis of a Bolt/Weld Group
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Bolt/Weld Group Subject to In-plane Loading
chunks.text: 17.11.1 Bolt/Weld Group Subject to In-plane Loading
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
17.11.1.1 General method of analysis
The design force in a bolt/weld or design force per unit length in a bolt/weld group subject to in-plane loading shall be determined in accordance with the following:
a) The connection plates shall be considered to be rigid and to rotate relative to each other about a point known as the instantaneous centre of rotation of the group;
b) In the case of a group subject to a pure couple only, the instantaneous centre of rotation coincides with the group centroid.  In the case of in-plane shear force applied at the group centroid, the instantaneous centre of the rotation is at infinity and the design force is uniformly distributed throughout the group. In all other cases, either the results of independent analyses for a pure couple alone and for an in-plane shear force applied at the group centroid shall be superposed, or a recognized method of analysis shall be used; and c) The design force in a bolt or design force per unit length at any point in the group shall be assumed to act at right angles to the radius from that point to the instantaneous centre, and shall be taken as proportional to that radius.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Bolt/Weld Group Subject to Out-of-Plane Loading
chunks.text: 17.11.2 Bolt/Weld Group Subject to Out-of-Plane Loading
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
17.11.2.1 General method of analysis
The design force of a bolt in bolt group or design force per unit length in the fillet weld group subject to out-ofplane loading shall be determined in accordance with the following:
a) Design force in the bolts or per unit length in the fillet weld group resulting from any shear force or axial force shall be considered to be equally shared by all bolts in the group or uniformly distributed over the length of the fillet weld group; and b) Design force resulting from a design bending moment shall be considered to vary linearly with distance from the relevant centroidal axes. The following shall also be considered:
1) in bearing type of bolt group plates in the compression side of the neutral axis and only bolts in the tension side of the neutral axis may be considered for calculating the neutral axis and second moment of area;
2) in the friction grip bolt group, only the bolts shall be considered in the calculation of neutral axis and second moment of area; and 3) the fillet weld group shall be considered in isolation from the connected element; for the calculation of centroid and second moment of the weld length.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
17.11.2.2 Alternative analysis
The design force per unit length in a fillet weld/bolt group may alternatively be determined by considering the fillet weld group as an extension of the connected member and distributing the design forces among the welds of the fillet weld group so as to satisfy equilibrium between the fillet weld group and the elements of the connected member.

17.11.3.1 General method of analysis
The design force in a bolt or per unit length of the weld shall be determined by the superposition of analysis for in-plane and out-of-plane cases discussed in 17.11.1 and 17.11.2.

chunks.text: 18.1 General
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Earthquake is a ‘displacement loading’ on a structure. This implies that ‘displacements’ are ‘imposed’
chunks.text:
18.1.1 Earthquake is a ‘displacement loading’ on a structure. This implies that ‘displacements’ are ‘imposed’
under a structure during earthquake shaking and ‘forces’ are induced in it. Thus, a structure is allowed to be designed to have lesser strength capacity than that required if it were to remain elastic. And, only chosen types of damage are permitted to be accrued in select components of a structure during strong earthquake shaking.
Thus, reliance is placed on the nonlinear response of a structure, especially on its deformation and ductility capacities. These must be achieved by adopting special design and detailing practices. Therefore, steel frames shall be so designed and detailed as to give them stability, and adequate stiffness, strength, and ductility capacities to resist severe earthquake shaking without collapse in all earthquake zones mentioned in 5 of Part C ‘Structural Design/Section 1 Loads and Load Effects’ of this NBCS.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Steel frames required to resist earthquake effects in all earthquake zones shall satisfy the requirements
chunks.text:
18.1.2 Steel frames required to resist earthquake effects in all earthquake zones shall satisfy the requirements
specified in good practice [C-6A(42)]. Frames are classified into two types, one which have minimal inelastic deformation and ductility capacities, called ordinary frames, and one with higher deformation and ductility capacities, called special frames. For earthquake zones III and above, only special frames are permitted to be used.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: For earthquake zone II, ordinary frames, namely ordinary moment frames (OMF) and ordinary
chunks.text:
18.1.3 For earthquake zone II, ordinary frames, namely ordinary moment frames (OMF) and ordinary
concentrically braced frames (OCBF), are permitted to be used. In design and detailing of OMFs and OCBFs, specific requirements of this Section shall be satisfied along with other provisions of this NBCS, in addition to the earthquake demand and design criteria requirements of 5 of Part C ‘Structural design/Section 1 Loads and Load Effects’ of this NBCS.

18.10 Ordinary Moment Frames (OMFs)
Ordinary moment frames (OMFs) of structural steel shall be designed to satisfy the requirements of this section.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
18.10.1 Basis of Design
Ordinary moment frames designed in accordance with these provisions are expected to possess limited inelastic deformation capacity through flexural yielding of the beams, panel zones, and columns.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
18.10.2 Analysis
When two moment frames oriented in orthogonal directions intersect, the possibility of beam yielding in both orthogonal directions simultaneously shall be considered in the estimation of design demand on the common column.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
18.10.3 Member Requirements
The requirements specified hereunder shall be satisfied by the component or member.

chunks.text:
18.10.3.1 Beams
Beam cross-section shall be plastic or compact, as defined in 10.8.2.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
18.10.3.2 Columns
Column cross-section shall be plastic or compact, as defined in 10.8.2.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
18.10.4 System Requirements
It is preferable to plan buildings to have independent lateral load resisting moment frames in the vertical plane along each principal plan direction. Also, the requirements given hereunder shall be satisfied by the building system.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
18.10.4.1 Beam-to-column connections
Beam-to-column connections may be rigid or semi-rigid moment connections, but shall satisfy the following criteria:
a) Rigid moment connections shall be designed to withstand a moment of at least 1.2 times of either the full plastic moment of the connected beam or the maximum moment that can be delivered by the beam to the joint due to the induced weakness at the ends of the beam, whichever is less.
b) Semi-rigid connections shall be designed and to withstand either a moment of at least 0.5 times the full plastic moment of the connected beam or the maximum moment that can be delivered by the system, whichever is less. The design moment shall be achieved within a rotation of 0.01 radians. The information given in Annex F may be used for checking.
c) The stiffness and strength of semi-rigid connections shall be accounted for in the design and the overall stability of the frame shall be ensured.
d) The rigid and semi-rigid connections shall be designed to withstand a shear resulting from the load combination 1.2 DL + 0.5 LL plus the shear corresponding to the design moment defined in (a) and (b), respectively.
e) In rigid fully welded connections, continuity plates of thickness equal to or greater than the thickness of the beam flange shall be provided and welded to the column flanges and web.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
18.10.4.2 Column to beam strength ratio
At a beam–column joint, strong column - weak beam design shall be adopted, suitably accounting for the reduction in moment capacity of columns due to axial load.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 19.2.2 Design Spectrum
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
19.2.2.1 Stress evaluation
Design stress shall be determined by elastic analysis of the structure to obtain stress resultants and the local stresses may be obtained by a conventional stress analysis method. The normal and shear stresses shall be determined considering all design actions on the members, but excluding stress concentration due to the geometry of the detail. The stress concentration effect is accounted for in detail category classification (see Table 26). The stress concentration, however, not characteristic of the detail shall be accounted for separately in the stress calculation.
In the fatigue design of trusses made of members with open sections, in which the end connections are not pinned, the stresses due to secondary bending moments shall be taken into account, unless the slenderness ratio (KL/r), of the member is greater than 40.
In the determination of stress range at the end connections between hollow sections, the effect of connection stiffness and eccentricities may be disregarded, provided:
a) the calculated stress range is multiplied by appropriate factor given in Table 24(A) in the case of circular hollow section connections and Table 24(B) in the case of rectangular hollow section connections; and b) the design throat thickness of fillet welds in the joints is greater than the wall thickness of the connected member.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
19.2.2.2 Design stress spectrum
In the case of loading events producing non-uniform stress range cycle, the stress spectrum may be obtained by a rational method, such as ‘rain flow counting’ or an equivalent method.

chunks.text: 20 DESIGN ASSISTED BY TESTING
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Testing of structural system, member or component shall be of the following categories:
chunks.text:
20.1.1 Testing of structural system, member or component shall be of the following categories:
a) Proof testing — The application of test loads to a structure, sub-structure, member or connection to ascertain the structural characteristics of only that specific unit; and b) Prototype testing — Testing of structures, sub-structures, members or connections is done to ascertain the structural characteristics of a class of such structures, sub-structures members or connection, which are nominally identical to the units tested.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 20.2 Types of Test
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
20.2.1 Acceptance Test
This is intended as a non-destructive test for confirming structural performance. It should be recognized that the loading applied to certain structures might cause permanent distortions.  Such effects do not necessarily indicate structural failure in acceptance test. However, the possibility of their occurrence should be agreed to before testing.
The load for acceptance test, Ftest,a  shall be determined from:
Ftest,a = (Self weight) + (1.15  Remainder of the permanent load) + (1.25  Variable load) The assembly shall satisfy the following criteria:
a) it shall demonstrate substantially linear behaviour under test loading; and b) on removal of the test load, the residual deflection shall not exceed 20 percent of the maximum-recorded deflection.
If the above criteria are not satisfied the test may be repeated one more time only, when the assembly shall satisfy the following criteria:
a) it shall demonstrate substantially linear behaviour on the second application of test loading; and b) corresponding recorded residual deflection in the second test shall not exceed 10 percent of the maximum deflection during the test.
PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 6 STEEL AND COMPOSITE CONSTRUCTION: 6(A) STEEL
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
20.2.2 Strength Test
Strength test is used to confirm the calculated resistance of a structure or component. Where a number of items are to be constructed to a common design, and one or more prototypes are tested to confirm their strength, the others may be accepted without any additional test, provided they are similar in all relevant respects to the prototype.
Before carrying out the strength test, the specimen should first be subjected to and satisfy the acceptance test.
Since the resistance of the assembly under test depends on the material properties, the actual yield strength of all the steel materials in the assembly shall be determined from coupon {test piece as defined in the accepted standard [C-6A(7)]} tests. The mean value of the yield strength, fym, taken from such tests shall be determined with due regard to the importance of each element in the assembly. The strength test load Ftest, s (including self weight) shall be determined from:
  y ym d mi s test, / f f F F   where Fd = factored design load for the ultimate limit state;
fy = characteristic yield stress of the material as assumed in the design; and mi = partial safety factor  for the  type  of  failure,  as  prescribed  in  this standard.
At this load there shall be no failure by buckling or rupture of any part of the structure or component tested. On removal of the test load, the deflection should decrease by at least 20 percent of the maximum deflection at Ftest,s.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
20.2.3 Test to Failure (Ultimate Strength Test)
The objective of a test to failure is to determine the design resistance from the ultimate resistance. In this situation it is still desirable to carry out the acceptance and strength tests, before test to failure. Not less than three tests shall be carried out on nominally identical specimens. An estimate should be made of the anticipated ultimate resistance as a basis for such tests. During a test to failure, the loading shall first be applied in increments up to the strength test load. Subsequent load increments shall then be determined from consideration of the principal load deflection plot. The test load resistance, Ftest.R shall be determined as that load at which the specimen is unable to sustain any further increase in load. At this load, gross permanent distortion is likely to have occurred and in some cases such large gross deformation may define the test limit. If the deviation of any individual test result exceeds 10 percent of the mean value obtained for all the three tests, at least three more tests shall be carried out. 20.2.4 Check Tests
Where a component or assembly is designed on the basis of strength tests or tests to failure and a production run is carried out of such items, an appropriate number of samples (not less than two) shall be selected from each production batch at random for check tests.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The samples shall be carefully examined to ensure that they are similar in all respects to the prototype
chunks.text:
20.2.4.1 The samples shall be carefully examined to ensure that they are similar in all respects to the prototype
tested, particular attention being given to the following:
a) Dimensions of components and connections;
b) Tolerance and workmanship; and c) Quality of steel used, checked with reference to mill test certificates.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Where it is not possible to determine either the variations or the effect of variations from the prototype,
chunks.text:
20.2.4.2 Where it is not possible to determine either the variations or the effect of variations from the prototype,
an acceptance test shall be carried out as a check test.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: In this check test, the deflections shall be measured at the same positions as in the acceptance test of the
chunks.text:
20.2.4.3 In this check test, the deflections shall be measured at the same positions as in the acceptance test of the
prototype.  The maximum measured deflection shall not exceed 120 percent of the deflection recorded during the acceptance test on the prototype and the residual deflection should not be more than 105 percent of that recorded for the prototype.

chunks.text: 20.4 Test Loading
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Where the self-weight of the specimen is not representative of the actual permanent load in service,
chunks.text:
20.4.1 Where the self-weight of the specimen is not representative of the actual permanent load in service,
allowance for the difference shall be made in the calculation of test loads to be applied.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: On the attainment of maximum load for either acceptance or strength tests, this load shall be maintained as
chunks.text:
20.4.2 On the attainment of maximum load for either acceptance or strength tests, this load shall be maintained as
given below. Reading of load and deflection shall be taken at intervals of 15 min and the loading shall be maintained constant until there is no significant increase in deflection during a 15 min period or until at least 1 h has elapsed after application of maximum load.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The test load shall be equal to the design load for the relevant limit state in proof testing.
chunks.text: 20.4.3 The test load shall be equal to the design load for the relevant limit state in proof testing.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: The test load in prototype testing shall be equal to the design load for the relevant limit state as multiplied
chunks.text:
20.4.4 The test load in prototype testing shall be equal to the design load for the relevant limit state as multiplied
by the appropriate factor given in Table 27.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 20.5 Criteria for Acceptance
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
20.5.1 Acceptance for Strength
The test structure, sub-structure, member or connection shall be deemed to comply with the requirements for strength if it is able to sustain the strength test load as required in 20.4.2.
It shall then be inspected to determine the nature and extent of any damage incurred during the test. The effects of the damage shall be considered and if necessary appropriate repairs to the damaged parts carried out.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
20.5.2 Acceptance for Serviceability
The maximum deformation of the structure or member under the serviceability limit state test load shall be within the serviceability limit values appropriate to the structure.

chunks.text: 21 DURABILITY
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
21.1 General
A durable steel structure is one that performs satisfactorily the desired function in the working environment under the anticipated exposure condition during its service life, without deterioration of the cross sectional area and loss of strength due to corrosion.
The material used, the detailing, fabrication, erection and surface protection measures should all address the corrosion protection and durability requirements.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 21.2 Requirements for Durability
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Shape, Size, Orientation of Members, Connections and Details
chunks.text:
21.2.1 Shape, Size, Orientation of Members, Connections and Details
The design, fabrication and erection details of exposed structures should be such that good drainage of water is ensured.  Standing pool of water, moisture accumulation and rundown of water for extended duration shall be avoided.
The details of connections should ensure that:
a) all exposed surfaces are easily accessible for inspection and maintenance; and b) all surfaces, not so easily accessible are completely sealed against ingress of moisture.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 21.2.2 Exposure Condition
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
21.2.2.1 General environment
The general environment, to which a steel structure is exposed during its working life is classified into five levels of severity, as given in Table 28.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
21.2.2.2 Abrasion
Specialist literature may be referred for durability of surfaces exposed to abrasive action as in machinery, conveyor belt support system, storage bins for grains or aggregates.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
21.2.2.3 Exposure to sulphate attack
Appropriate coatings may be used when surfaces of structural steel are exposed to concentration of sulphates (SO3) in soil, ground water, etc.
When exposed to very high sulphate concentrations of more than 2 percent in soil and 5 percent in water, some form of lining such as polyethylene, polychloroprene sheet or surface coating based on asphalt, chlorinated rubber, epoxy or polymethane material should be used to completely avoid access of the solution to the steel surface.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 21.2.4 Surface Protection
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: In the case of mild exposure, a coat of primer after removal of any loose mill scale may be adequate.  As
chunks.text:
21.2.4.1 In the case of mild exposure, a coat of primer after removal of any loose mill scale may be adequate.  As
the exposure condition becomes more critical, more elaborate surface preparations and coatings become necessary. In case of extreme environmental classification, protection shall be as per specialist literature.
Table 29 gives guidance to protection of steelwork for different desired lives.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Steel surfaces shall be provided with at least one coat of primer immediately after its surface preparation,
chunks.text:
21.2.4.2 Steel surfaces shall be provided with at least one coat of primer immediately after its surface preparation,
such as by sand blasting to remove all mill scale and rust and to expose the steel.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Steel without protective coating shall not be stored for long duration in outdoor environment.
chunks.text: 21.2.4.3 Steel without protective coating shall not be stored for long duration in outdoor environment.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Surfaces to transfer forces by friction as in HSFG connections shall not be painted.  However, it shall be
chunks.text:
21.2.4.4 Surfaces to transfer forces by friction as in HSFG connections shall not be painted.  However, it shall be
ensured that moisture is not trapped on such surfaces after pre-tensioning of bolts by proper protective measures.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Members to be assembled by welding shall not be pre-painted at regions adjacent to the location of such
chunks.text:
21.2.4.5 Members to be assembled by welding shall not be pre-painted at regions adjacent to the location of such
welds.  However, after welding, appropriate protective coatings shall be applied in the region, as required by the exposure conditions. If the contact surfaces cannot be properly protected against ingress of moisture by surface coating, they may be completely sealed by appropriate welds.
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Pre-painted members shall be protected against abrasion of the coating during transportation, handling
chunks.text:
21.2.4.6 Pre-painted members shall be protected against abrasion of the coating during transportation, handling
and erection.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
21.2.5 Special Steels
Steels with special alloying elements and production process to obtain better corrosion resistance may be used as per specialist literature.

chunks.text:
22.1 Requirements
The requirements shall apply to steel building elements designed to exhibit a required fire-resistance level (FRL) as per the relevant specifications. The provisions of this section are quite rudimentary and simplistic. Specialist literature for design of steel structures for fire resistance and design based on testing may be necessary for a more comprehensive design of steel buildings to resist fire.

chunks.section_title: Determination of Period of Structural Adequacy
chunks.text:
22.3.2 Determination of Period of Structural Adequacy
The period of structural adequacy (PSA) shall be determined using one of the following methods:
a) By calculation:
1) determining the limiting temperature of the steel (Tl) in accordance with 22.5; and 2) determining the PSA as the time (t) (in min) from the start of the test to the time at which the limiting steel temperature is attained, in accordance with 22.6 for protected members and 22.7 for unprotected members.
b) By direct application of a single test in accordance with 22.8; or c) By calculation of the temperature of the steel member by using a rational method of analysis confirmed by test data or by methods available in specialist literature.

chunks.text:
22.5 Limiting Steel Temperature
The limiting steel temperature (Tl), in °C, in the case of structural steels, shall be calculated by substituting fy, fu, E, and G values with fy(T), fy(T), E(T), and G(T) calculated in accordance with 22.4, respectively in 13, 14, 15, and 16 to calculate the design capacity of the member as a function of steel temperature. The limiting temperature (Tl) will be the temperature at which the design capacity is equal to the design action on the member.
The design action under fire shall consider the following:
a) Loads as per the load combinations for fire conditions given in Table 4;
b) Effects of restraint to expansion of the elements during fire; and c) Reduced bond likely under fire.
Limiting steel temperature for special steels may be appropriately calculated using the thermal characteristics of the material obtained from the supplier of the steel.

chunks.text: 23 SUSTAINABLE STEEL CONSTRUCTION
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
23.1 General
This Chapter specifies general requirements and practices for achieving environmentally sustainable steelwork building construction. This supplements the requirements of the other chapters of this specification.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Specification Requirements from Supply Chain Members
chunks.text: 23.3 Specification Requirements from Supply Chain Members
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
23.3.2 Requirements from Main Contractor
a) Early engagement of supply chain and subcontractors with emphasis on sustainability; and b) Judicious site planning to receive material, use of labour and location of machinery for efficient handling and construction.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
23.3.4 Requirements from Steelwork Contractor
Establish a carbon reduction plan in steelwork. This may include use of low carbon emission transport, maximize the steelwork loads, optimizing haulage routes, minimizing empty runs, etc.
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 23.4 Sustainable Design
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
23.4.1 General
The environmental impacts associated with steelwork building construction be greatly reduced during the design process by:
a) reducing the material in the structure;
b) minimizing fabrication, and avoidance of maintenance during service life; and c) Identifying environmental improvements at the conceptual design stage requires the involvement of all the stakeholders such as architects, steelwork contractor during all design stages. Collaborative design processes result in:
1) materials being used more efficiently;
2) fewer on-site changes; and 3) reduced environmental impacts.
Greenhouse gas or carbon emissions currently being the priority, action is required by all parts of the supply chain for the sector to decarbonize in line with global targets. This includes supply-side measures, in particularly decarbonizing steel-making and also demand-side measures including more efficient design and design for longevity, deconstruction and reuse.
Greenhouse gas emission should be based on life cycle assessment, which should include emissions in material manufacturing, transport, fabrication, erection, finishing, commissioning, maintenance during life and finally at the end of useful life deconstruction and disposal of the materials as waste or through recycling and reuse.
Further, environmentally friendly designs should be implemented in the construction projects and pollution of the environment during the process of construction should be avoided, if not minimized.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
23.4.3 Design for Adaptability and Deconstruction
Design engineer should review design options with the steelwork contractor that may contribute to future flexibility, adaptability, deconstruction and reuse of the building structure, such as:
a) how the building design and information records about the materials and members can facilitate future, remodelling, deconstruction and recovery for reuse and recycling;
b) ensuring accessibility to members and connections to allow for deconstruction and for ease of strengthening in the future; and c) greater standardization of sections sizes, lengths and connections, if appropriate from adaptability and deconstruction.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

23.5.4.1 Untreated steelwork
Any part of the steelwork such as steelwork in a less corrosivity category, that is to be left untreated shall be identified in the Project Specification.

23.5.4.2 Paint systems
The protective coating system shall satisfy the requirements given in 21.

chunks.text:
23.5.4.3 Intumescent systems
For the same fire resistance water-based acrylic intumescent likely to have a lower environmental impact, when compared to solvent-based acrylic intumescent.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
23.5.4.4 Hot-dip galvanizing
Requirements for thicker coatings, for example, by prior grit blasting, should be avoided by prior assessment of the predicted galvanized coating life and the minimum thickness required to avoid over-specification. For certain steel members (for example, with higher reactivity during galvanizing and/or larger section thickness), thicker coatings may also be achieved without grit blasting. Design and fabrication considerations for hot dip galvanizing should ensure adequate drainage and optimize material efficiency. Plan should optimize transport distances and provide direct delivery to the construction works, where feasible.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 24 FABRICATION AND ERECTION
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.1 General
Tolerances for fabrication of steel structures shall conform to the accepted standard [C-6A(44)]. Tolerances for erection of steel structures shall conform to the accepted standard [C-6A(45)]. For general guidance on fabrication by welding, reference may be made to good practice [C-6A(46)]. In addition to the above, the following requirements shall also be considered:
a) The designer shall, in conjunction with the floor framing and vertical framing/stacking arrangements of the project, provide suitable tolerance mitigation measures. Such measures may include the use of slotted or oversized holes in beams and columns, use of HSFG bolts, or other appropriate detailing. These provisions need not be adopted for all members; however, they shall be judiciously incorporated in selected connections and splices to achieve the desired tolerance accommodation. PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 6 STEEL AND COMPOSITE CONSTRUCTION: 6(A) STEEL
b) The structural designer shall coordinate with other disciplines, such as façade, building services, and transportation systems, and ensure that the specified tolerances for steel structures are compatible with their requirements. Where the design necessitates tolerances more stringent than those specified in the relevant codes, such requirements shall be clearly indicated in the drawings and specifications. However, in no case shall the specified tolerances be more stringent than the applicable mill rolling tolerances. c) The designer shall specify the permissible overall horizontal and vertical tolerances for the completed building structure, in accordance with the design intent. While [C-6A(45)] specifies tolerances for erected elements, it does not address the overall geometrical accuracy of the completed structure. Therefore, the structural designer shall, in coordination with the architect and other relevant disciplines, define the acceptable limits of overall as-built accuracy.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

These limits shall be clearly specified so as to enable proper planning and execution by the contractor at all stages of construction.

chunks.text: 24.2 Fabrication Procedures
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.2.1 Straightening
Material shall be straightened or formed to the specified configuration by methods that will not reduce the properties of the material below the values used in design. Local application of pressure at room or at elevated temperature or other thermal means may be used for straightening, provided the above is satisfied.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.2.2 Clearances
The erection clearance for cleated ends of members, connecting steel to steel should preferably be not greater than
2.0 mm at each end. The erection clearance at ends of beams without web cleats should be not more than 3 mm
at each end. Where for practical reasons, greater clearance is necessary, suitably designed seating should be provided.

chunks.text:
24.2.3 Cutting
Cutting shall be effected by sawing, shearing, cropping, machining or thermal cutting process.  Shearing, cropping and gas cutting shall be clean, reasonably square, and free from any distortion. Should the inspector find it necessary, the edges shall be ground after cutting. Planning or finishing of sheared or gas-cut edges of plates or shapes shall not be required, unless specially noted on drawing or included in stipulated edge preparation for welding or when specifically required in the following section.
Re-entrant corners shall be free from notches and shall have largest practical radii with a minimum radius of
15 mm.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.2.3.1 Shearing
Shearing of items over 16 mm thick to be galvanized and subject to tensile force or bending moment shall not be carried out, unless the item is stress relieved subsequently.
The use of sheared edges in the tension area shall be avoided in location subject to plastic hinge rotation at factored loading.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.2.3.2 Thermal cutting
Gas cutting of high tensile steel by mechanically controlled torch may be permitted, provided special care is taken to leave sufficient metal to be removed by machining, so that all metal that has been hardened by flame is removed.
Hand flame cutting may be permitted only subject to the approval of the inspecting authority.
Except where the material is subsequently joined by welding, no load shall be transmitted through a gas cut surface.
NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
Thermally cut free edges, which shall be subject to calculated static tensile stress shall be free from round bottom gouges greater than 5 mm deep. Gouges greater than 5 mm deep and notches shall be removed by grinding.

chunks.text: 24.2.4 Holing
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Holes through more than one thickness of material for members, such as compound stanchion and girder
chunks.text:
24.2.4.1 Holes through more than one thickness of material for members, such as compound stanchion and girder
flanges, shall be where possible, drilled after the members are assembled and tightly clamped or bolted together.
A round hole for a bolt shall either be machine flame cut, or drilled full size, or sub-punched 3 mm undersize and reamed to size or punched full size.
Hand flame cutting of a bolt hole shall not be permitted except as a site rectification measure for holes in column base plates.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.2.4.2 Punching
A punched hole shall be permitted only in material whose yield stress (fy) does not exceed 360 MPa and where thickness does not exceed (5600/fy) mm. In cyclically loaded details, punching shall be avoided in plates with thickness greater than 12 mm.
For greater thickness and cyclically loaded details, holes shall be either drilled from the solid or sub-punched or sub drilled and reamed.
The die for all sub-punched holes or the drill for all sub-drilled holes shall be at least 3 mm smaller than the required diameter of finished hole.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.2.4.3 Oversize holes
A special plate washer of minimum thickness 4 mm shall be used under the nut, if the hole diameter is larger than the bolt diameter by 3 mm or more.
Oversize hole shall not exceed 1.25d or (d + 8) mm in diameter, were d is the nominal bolt diameter, in mm.
A short slotted hole shall not exceed the appropriate hole size in width and 1.33d, in length. A long slotted hole shall not exceed the appropriate hole size in width and 2.5d, in length.  If the slot length is larger than those specified, shear transfer in the direction of slot is not admissible even in friction type of connection.
Slotted holes shall be punched either in one operation or else formed by punching or drilling two round holes apart and completed by high quality mechanically controlled flame cutting and dressing to ensure that bolt can freely travel the full length of the slot.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.2.4.4 Fitted bolt holes
Holes for turned and fitted bolts shall be drilled to a diameter equal to the nominal diameter of the shank or barrel subject to tolerance specified in the accepted standards [C-6A(47)]. Preferably, parts to be connected with close tolerance or barrel bolts shall be firmly held together by tacking bolts or clamps and the holes drilled through all the thicknesses at one operation and subsequently reamed to size.  All holes not drilled through all thicknesses at one operation shall be drilled to a smaller size and reamed out after assembly. Where this is not practicable, the parts shall be drilled and reamed separately through hard bushed steel jigs.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Holes for rivets or bolts shall not be formed generally by gas cutting process. However, advanced gas
chunks.text:
24.2.4.5 Holes for rivets or bolts shall not be formed generally by gas cutting process. However, advanced gas
cutting processes such as plasma cutting may be used to make holes in statically loaded members only. In cyclically loaded members subjected to tensile stresses which are vulnerable under fatigue, gas cutting shall not be used unless subsequent reaming is done to remove the material in the heat affected zone around the hole.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.3 Assembly
All parts of bolted members shall be pinned or bolted and rigidly held together during assembly.
The component parts shall be assembled and aligned in such a manner that they are neither twisted nor otherwise damaged, and shall be so prepared that the specified camber, if any, is provided.
PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 6 STEEL AND COMPOSITE CONSTRUCTION: 6(A) STEEL
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.3.1 Holes in Assembly
When holes are drilled in one operation through two or more separable parts, these parts, when so specified by the engineer, shall be separated after drilling and the burrs removed.
Matching holes for rivets and black bolts shall register with each other so that a gauge of 1.5 mm or 2.0 mm (as the case may be, depending on whether the diameter of the rivet or bolt is less than or more than 25 mm) less in diameter than the diameter of the hole will pass freely through the assembled members in the direction at right angle to such members.
Drilling done during assembly to align holes shall not distort the metal or enlarge the holes.
Holes in adjacent part shall match sufficiently well to permit easy entry of bolts. If necessary, holes except oversize or slotted holes may be enlarged to admit bolts, by moderate amount of reaming.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.3.2 Thread Length
When design is based on bolts with unthreaded shanks in the shear plane, appropriate measures shall be specified to ensure that, after allowing for tolerance, neither the threads nor the thread run-out be in the shear plane.
The length of bolt shall be such that at least one clear thread shows above the nut and at least one thread plus the thread run out is clear beneath the nut after tightening. One washer shall be provided under the rotated part.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.3.3 Assembly Subjected to Vibration
When non-preloaded bolts are used in a structure subject to vibration, the nuts shall be secured by locking devices or other mechanical means. The nuts of preloaded bolts may be assumed to be sufficiently secured by the normal tightening procedure.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
24.3.4 Washers
Washers are not normally required on non-preloaded bolts, unless specified otherwise. Tapered washers shall be used where the surface is inclined at more than 3° to a plane perpendicular to the bolt axis.
Hardened washer shall be used for preloaded bolts or the nut, whichever is to be rotated.
All material within the grip of the bolt shall be steel and no compressible material shall be permitted in the grip.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Column splices and butt joints of struts and compression members, depending on contact for stress
chunks.text:
24.7.1 Column splices and butt joints of struts and compression members, depending on contact for stress
transmission, shall be accurately machined and close-butted over the whole section with a clearance not exceeding
0.2 mm locally, at any place. Sum of all such clearance shall not be more than 30 percent of the contact area for
stress transmission. In column caps and bases, the ends of shafts together with the attached gussets, angles, channels, etc; after connecting together should be accurately machined so that clearance between the contact surfaces shall not exceed 2 mm locally, subject further to the condition that sum total of all such clearance shall not exceed 30 percent of the total contact area for stress transmission. Care should be taken that these gussets, connecting angles or channels are fixed with such accuracy that they are not reduced in thickness by machining by more than 2.0 mm.

chunks.section_title: Where sufficient gussets and rivets or welds are provided to transmit the entire loading (see provisions
chunks.text:

ANNEX B
[Clauses 11.1.1(c) and 11.7.2.1(b)] ANALYSIS AND DESIGN METHODS B-1 ADVANCED STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS AND DESIGN B-1.1 Analysis For a frame, comprising members of compact section with full lateral restraint, an advanced structural analysis may be carried out, provided the analysis can be shown to accurately model the actual behaviour of that class of frames. The analysis shall take into account the relevant material properties, residual stresses, geometrical imperfections, reduction in stiffness due to axial compression, second-order effects, section strength and ductility, erection procedures and interaction with the foundations. Advanced structural analysis for earthquake loads shall take into account provisions of 5 of Part C ‘Strucutral design/Section 1 Loads and Load Effects’ of this NBCS. B-1.2 Design For the strength limit state, it shall be sufficient to satisfy the section capacity requirements given under 15 for the members subjected to bending, under 14 for axial members, under 16 for combined forces and under 17 for connections. Effect of moment magnification given in 16, instability given in 14 and lateral buckling given in 15 need not be considered while designing the member, since advanced analysis methods directly consider these. B-2 SECOND ORDER ELASTIC ANALYSIS AND DESIGN B-2.1 Analysis In a second-order elastic analysis, the members shall be assumed to remain elastic, and changes in frame geometry under the design load and changes in the effective stiffness of the members due to axial forces shall be accounted for. In a frame where the elastic buckling load factor (cr) of the frame as determined in accordance with 11.6 is greater than 5, the changes in the effective stiffness of the members due to axial forces may be neglected. NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS 2026
B-2.2 Design Bending Moment The design bending moment under factored load shall be taken as the maximum bending moment in the length of the member.

B-3 FRAME INSTABILITY ANALYSIS B-3.1 Analysis Frame instability, as treated here, is related to the design of multi-storey rigid-jointed frames subject to side sway. The elastic critical load factor, cr may be determined using the deflection method as given in B-3.2 or any other recognized method. This is used to calculate the amplified sway moments for elastic designs and to check frame stability in plastic designs. The elastic critical load factor, cr of a frame is the ratio by which each of the factored loads would have to be increased to cause elastic instability. B-3.2 Deflection Method An accurate method of analysis (ordinary linear elastic analysis) should be used to determine the horizontal deflections of the frame due to horizontal forces applied at each floor level, which is equal to the notional horizontal load in 11.3.6. Allowance should be made for the degree of rigidity of the base as given in B-3.2 in this deflection calculation. The base stiffness should be determined by reference to 11.3.4.

ANNEX F
(Clauses 11.2.1.2, 15.6.4.2, 17.6.1, 18.10.4.1 and 18.11.2.1) CONNECTIONS F-1 GENERAL The requirement for the design of splice and beam to column connection as well as recommendation for their design shall be as given below. F-2 BEAM SPLICES F-2.1 For rolled section beam splices located away from the point of maximum moment, it may be assumed that the flange splice carries all the moment and the web splice carries the shear (see Fig. 30). However, in the case of a deep girder, the total moment may be divided between the flange and the web in accordance with the stress distribution. The web connection should then be designed to resist its share of moment and shear. Even web splice is designed to carry only shear force, the moment about the centroid of the bolt group on either side of the splice should be designed for moment due to eccentricity. F-2.2 Flange joints should preferably not be located at points of maximum stress. Where splice plates are used, their area shall not be less than 5 percent in excess of the area of the flange element spliced; and their centre of gravity shall coincide, as nearly as possible with that of the element spliced. There shall be enough fasteners on each side of the splice to develop the load in the element spliced plus 5 percent but in no case should the strength developed be less than 50 percent of the effective strength of the material spliced. Wherever possible in welded construction, flange plates shall be joined by complete penetration butt welds. These butt welds shall develop the full strength of the plates. Whenever the flange width or thickness changes at the splice location, gradual transition shall be made in the width/thickness of the larger flange. F-2.3 When beam splice is located at the point of inflection of a continuous beam, the flange splicing requirement given above may be relaxed appropriately.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text:
F-3 COLUMN SPLICE F-3.1 Where the ends of compression members are faced for bearing over the whole area, they shall be spliced to hold the connected parts aligned. The ends of compression members faced for bearing shall invariably be machined to ensure perfect contact of surfaces in bearing (see Fig. 31). F-3.2 Where such members are not faced for complete bearing the splices shall be designed to transmit all the forces to which the members is subjected at the splice location. FIG. 30 BEAM SPLICES PART C STRUCTURAL DESIGN — SECTION 6 STEEL AND COMPOSITE CONSTRUCTION: 6(A) STEEL
F-3.3 Wherever possible, splices shall be proportioned and arranged so that centroidal axis of the splice coincides as nearly as possible with the centroidal axes of the members joined, in order to avoid eccentricity; but where eccentricity is present in the joint, the resulting stress considering eccentricity shall be provided for. F-3.4 If a column flange is subjected to significant tension or if the faces are not prepared for bearing, or if full continuity is required without slip, only HSFG bolts shall be used. F-4 BEAM-TO-COLUMN CONNECTIONS F-4.1 Simple Connections Simple connections are assumed to transfer only shear at some nominal eccentricity and typically used in frames up to about five stories in height, where strength rather than stiffness govern the design. In such frames separate lateral load resisting system is to be provided in the form of bracings or shear walls. The connections shown in Fig. 32 (A), Fig. 32 (B), Fig. 32 (C) and Fig. 32 (D) can be assumed as simple connections in framed analysis and need to be checked only for the transfer of shear from beam to column. F-4.2 Rigid Connections In high-rise and slender structures, stiffness requirements may warrant the use of rigid connections. Rigid connections transfer significant moments to the columns and are assumed to undergo negligible deformations at the joint.

F-4.3 Semi-Rigid Connections Semi-rigid connections fall between the two types mentioned above. The fact is that simple connections do have some degree of rotational rigidity as in the semi-rigid connections. Similarly, rigid connections do experience some degree of joint deformation and this can be utilized to reduce the joint design moments. The moment-rotation relationship of the connections have to be determined based on experiments conducted for the specific design or based on the relationship derived from tests, presented in specialist literature. The simplest method of analysis will be to idealize the connection as an equivalent rotational spring with either a bilinear or non-linear moment-rotation characteristics. The classification proposed by Bjorhovde combined with the Frye-Morris model can be used with convenience to model semi-rigid connections, as given in the next section. F-4.3.1 Connection Classification Connections are classified according to their ultimate strength or in terms of their initial elastic stiffness and Bjorhovde’s classification. It is based on the non-dimensional moment parameter (m1 = Mu / Mpb) and the nondimensional rotation parameter ( 1 =   r/p), where p is the plastic rotation. The Bjorhovde’s classification is based on a reference length of the beam equal to 5 times the depth of the beam.

F-5 COLUMN BASES F-5.1 Base Plates Columns shall be provided with base plates capable of distributing the compressive forces in the compressed parts of the column over a bearing area such that the bearing pressure on the foundation does not exceed the design strength of the point. The design strength of the joint between the base plate and the foundation shall be determined taking account of the material properties and dimensions of both the grout and the concrete foundation. F-5.2 Holding Down Bolts (Anchor Bolts) F-5.2.1 Holding down bolts shall be provided if necessary to resist the effects of the design loads. They shall be designed to resist tension due to uplift forces and tension due to bending moments as appropriate. F-5.2.2 When calculating the tension forces due to bending moments, the lever arm shall not be taken as more than the distance between the centroid of the bearing area on the compression side and the centroid of the bolt group on the tension side, taking the tolerances on the positions of the holding down bolts into account.

H-9 MAINTENANCE H-9.1 General Where steelwork is to be encased in solid concrete, brickwork or masonry, the question of maintenance should not arise, but where steelwork is to be housed in hollow fire protection or is to be unprotected, particularly where the steelwork is exposed to a corroding agent, the question of painting or protective treatment of the steelwork should be given careful consideration at the construction stage, having regard to the special circumstances of the case. H-9.2 Connections Where connections are exposed to a corroding agent, they should be periodically inspected, and any corroded part should be thoroughly cleaned and painted. Where bolted connections are not solidly encased and are subject to vibratory effects of machinery or plant, they should be periodically inspected and all bolts tightened. National Building Code Sectional Committee, CED 46 FOREWORD This NBCS (Part C/Subsection 6B) covers the composite construction consists of the use of prefabricated steel structural units like steel beams and steel open web joists (trusses) in combination with concrete elements and often with steel reinforcements. The design and construction should ensure monolithic action between the structural steel and concrete components so that they act as a single structural unit. The Section 6 ‘Steel’ was first published in 1970 and was subsequently revised in 1983, 2005 and 2016 as a chapter of the National Building Code of India. In the second revision in 2005, the detailed design provisions were not included as IS 800 : 1984 ‘Code of practice for general construction in steel (second revision)’was under revision at that time. This Section, therefore, then referred to the 1984 version of IS 800 with the remarks that the latest version would prevail, as and when published. It, however, covered the philosophical aspects of limit state design which was being introduced in the revision of IS 800. IS 800 was subsequently revised and published as IS 800 : 2007 and hence, became the prevailing version for use under this Section. In the third revision of 2016, the Section 6 was brought in line with the revised version of IS 800 : 2007 and its amendment No. 1 and to take care of further improvements and incorporations required. In the current revision, this publication has been renamed as National Building Construction Standards (NBCS).

In this revision of Section 6, the Section has been subdivided into the following subsections with the chapter on ‘composite construction in structural steel and concrete’ being introduced for the first time:
a) 6A Steel; and b) 6B Composite construction in structural steel and concrete. The provisions of this Subsection (Part C/Subsection 6B) are largely based on IS 11384 : 2022 ‘Composite construction in structural steel and concrete — Code of practice (first revision)’. The growing use of steelconcrete composites in building construction necessitated this new chapter in this NBCS. The provisions of this Subsection conform to the limit state design philosophy, ensuring consistency with IS 456 : 2000 ‘Plain and reinforced concrete — Code of practice’ for reinforced concrete and Part C/Sec  6A for structural steel. The Subsection includes comprehensive provisions for the design of key structural components such as beams, slabs, and columns in composite construction. It specifically addresses two types of composite columns — Concrete-encased steel columns, which may be either fully or partially encased, and concrete-filled steel columns — Both of which enhance load-bearing capacity and fire resistance. For composite slabs, the Subsection includes two types: profiled sheeting, which serves as formwork for reinforced concrete, and embossed profile sheeting, which functions as both formwork and tension reinforcement, with or without shear connectors. It also provides guidelines for the design and testing of shear connectors to ensure efficient load transfer. Serviceability limit states regulate deflection, vibration, and fire performance. Additionally, the subsection includes specifications for light gauge steel and lightweight concrete, broadening the scope of composite construction applications. This subsection is restricted to the design of steel-concrete composite components and systems used in buildings.

All requirements of Part C/Sec  6A in so far as they apply, shall be deemed to form a part of this subsection, except where otherwise laid down in this subsection. As the regulation of land development and buildings is a State subject and is dealt by the States and local bodies such as urban local bodies within their jurisdiction through building regulatory documents like building regulations, building byelaws, and fire regulations, this document is voluntary in nature and is non-binding. The implementation depends on adoption by concerned parties or stipulations in a contract or by appropriate adoption by the concerned authorities. For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this Subsection is complied with the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2 : 2022 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical values (second revision)’. The number of significant places retained in the rounded-off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this Subsection.

At the time of publication, the editions indicated in the standards were valid. All standards are subject to revision and parties to agreements based on any Part/Section are encouraged to investigate the possibility of applying the most recent editions of the standards. In the list of standards given at the end of a Part/Section, the number appearing within parentheses in the first column indicates the number of the reference of the standard in the Part/Section. 3 TERMINOLOGY
For the purpose of this Subsection, the definitions given in as per good practices [C-6B(1)] and the following shall apply.

chunks.section_title: Accidental Load — The load is not normally expected in design life but has a major impact if it ever occurs,
chunks.text:
3.1 Accidental Load — The load is not normally expected in design life but has a major impact if it ever occurs,
such as ramming of vehicles against columns or any other member of the frame like bracings, blast loading, etc.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Accompanying Load — Imposed load acting along with leading imposed load but causing lower action
chunks.text:
3.2 Accompanying Load — Imposed load acting along with leading imposed load but causing lower action
and/or deflections.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Action — The primary cause for stress or deformations in a structure, such as dead, imposed, wind, seismic,
chunks.text:
3.3 Action — The primary cause for stress or deformations in a structure, such as dead, imposed, wind, seismic,
or temperature loads.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Built-up Section — A member fabricated by inter-connecting more than one element to form a compound
chunks.text:
3.4 Built-up Section — A member fabricated by inter-connecting more than one element to form a compound
section acting as a single member.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Camber — intentionally introduced pre-curving (generally upwards) in a system, member or any portion of a
chunks.text:
3.5 Camber — intentionally introduced pre-curving (generally upwards) in a system, member or any portion of a
member with respect to its chord. These are generally introduced to compensate for deflections at a specific level of loads.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Composite Action — Integral action of primary supporting steel member and supported concrete deck with
chunks.text:
3.6 Composite Action — Integral action of primary supporting steel member and supported concrete deck with
or without limited slip at their interface to ensure greater strength and rigidity. In composite columns, it is the integral action between steel and its encasement or infill concrete. The shear transfer is to be ensured through the use of mechanical devices known as shear connectors in composite beams and columns, as required (see Fig. 8).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Design Load/Factored Load — A load value obtained by multiplying the characteristic load with the partial
chunks.text:
3.7 Design Load/Factored Load — A load value obtained by multiplying the characteristic load with the partial
safety factor for loads.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Design Service Life — The time period during which the structure or its components should satisfy the design
chunks.text:
3.8 Design Service Life — The time period during which the structure or its components should satisfy the design
objectives and functions.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Detail Category — Designation given to a particular detail to indicate the S-N curve to be used in fatigue
chunks.text:
3.9 Detail Category — Designation given to a particular detail to indicate the S-N curve to be used in fatigue
assessment.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Differential Shrinkages — It is entirely due to shrinkage of concrete from the time composite action comes
chunks.text:
3.10 Differential Shrinkages — It is entirely due to shrinkage of concrete from the time composite action comes
into effect. When the coefficient of thermal expansion varies significantly between steel and concrete (concrete with limestone or granite aggregate), it also includes the difference in thermal strain between the steel and concrete. Differential shrinkage may lead to an increase in stresses and is more pronounced in continuous beams.

element.

chunks.section_title: Flexible Shear Connector — It resists shear forces by bending, tension or shearing in the root at the
chunks.text:
3.14 Flexible Shear Connector — It resists shear forces by bending, tension or shearing in the root at the
connection point of the steel member. It is subjected to plastic deformations as it reaches the ultimate strength, and the failure mode is ductile. It consists of studs, channels, etc (Fig. 8) welded to steel members to develop composite action with the concrete.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Initial Dead Load — The combination of weight of steel structure and the portion of the concrete deck that
chunks.text:
3.15 Initial Dead Load — The combination of weight of steel structure and the portion of the concrete deck that
is supported by the steel structure alone before the development of full composite action with concrete reaching
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.text: 75 percent of its 28 days strength.

chunks.section_title: Loads — Applied forces as per loads indicated in relevant standards (see Part C ‘Structural Design/
chunks.text:

Section 1 Loads and Load effects’ of this NBCS) for dead, imposed, wind, snow loads, etc, and also for seismic loads that the structure is subjected to during its lifetime.

chunks.section_title: Partial Safety Factor for Loads — The factors multiplied by the loads or their combinations to obtain
chunks.text:
3.18 Partial Safety Factor for Loads — The factors multiplied by the loads or their combinations to obtain
design loads while checking performance under various limit states.
3.19 m-k Factors — Physically, in a composite slab, ‘m’ is a broad measure of the mechanical interlock between
the embossed profiled decking sheet and the reinforced cement concrete on top of the deck, and ‘k’ represents the frictional resistance between the two elements that is, steel and concrete (see Fig. 38).
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Rigid Shear Connectors — These are shear hoops welded to bars, angles, horseshoes or tees welded to
chunks.text:
3.20 Rigid Shear Connectors — These are shear hoops welded to bars, angles, horseshoes or tees welded to
the flange of the fabricated steel units, as shown in Fig. 8(b) and Fig. 8 (c). They resist shear forces by concrete bearing on the vertical face and shearing. They exhibit negligible deformation under shear transfer (that is, brittle failure). These are not usually recommended for ultimate limit state design.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS

chunks.section_title: Service Limit — The loading state beyond which the structure or its components becomes incapable of
chunks.text:
3.21 Service Limit — The loading state beyond which the structure or its components becomes incapable of
performing its intended function due to excessive deformation, or deflection, or vibration.
chunks.title: NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION STANDARDS
